fd01981ce4d3df94: KUALA LUMPUR: Halal Development Corporation Bhd (HDC) will help Palestinian businesses tap Malaysia's halal market.
This follows the recognition of the Palestine Standards Institution (PSI) by the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia (Jakim) as a recognised foreign halal certification body.
HDC chairman Prof Dr Mohd Afandi Salleh said the priority now was to turn the recognition into tangible business opportunities.
This is by helping Palestinian producers understand local market requirements, connect with buyers and distributors, and prepare their products for entry.
He said HDC will work with relevant partners to facilitate industry engagement and commercial connections.
Malaysia's halal exports reached RM68.52 billion in 2025, up 10.9 per cent from a year earlier.
Food and beverages accounted for RM36.86 billion, or 53.8 per cent, while halal ingredients contributed RM21.39 billion, or 31.2 per cent.
Afandi said the recognition covered eligible products including food and beverages, raw materials, cosmetics, personal care products and pharmaceuticals, subject to applicable requirements.
He also acknowledged the Malaysian International Chamber of Commerce and Industry's role in facilitating engagement between PSI, HDC and Jakim.

However, he stressed that halal certification recognition alone did not guarantee market entry, as businesses must also comply with Malaysia's import, product safety, labelling and other regulatory requirements.

Afandi said trade could complement humanitarian assistance by helping Palestinian businesses sustain their operations and livelihoods, while creating commercial opportunities that meet Malaysia's halal and regulatory standards.
a577b73295ede057: GEORGE TOWN: Work on the second and third Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency's offshore patrol vessels (OPV), which has long been suspended, will begin again soon.
MMEA director-general Admiral Datuk Mohd Rosli Abdullah said the work would be carried out by a new company in Miri and Sibu.

"The construction process is expected to take a maximum of 36 months to complete, as it includes the requirement to move the vessels from Klang to Sarawak," he told a press conference in conjunction with the MMEA Media Engagement Day 2026 programme here.
Previously, it was reported that the original procurement contract for the three OPVs was mutually terminated with THHE Destini Sdn Bhd on Dec 31, 2024.
OPV 1, named KM Tun Fatimah, was successfully handed over to MMEA on Jan 2, 2024, while the completion costs for the remaining two vessels were revised by the Home Ministry to RM319.58 million.

On the agency's modernisation plans, Rosli said MMEA had received approval for an allocation totalling RM1.088 billion for 16 projects under the Second Rolling Plan of the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP) for 2027.
He said, of the total allocation, RM339.94 million had been earmarked for physical projects, including the construction of the Johor Malaysian Maritime Complex in Mukim Tanjung Kupang.
0512ed2052abd010: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 — The Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) has issued an evening thunderstorm warning across large swathes of Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah, and Sarawak until 8.00pm today, a day after torrential downpours triggered widespread flash floods across the Klang Valley.

The weather alert, released at 4.10pm, warns of severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, and gusty winds, placing commuters and low-lying neighbourhoods on high alert following Monday’s evening travel chaos.

In the peninsula, the advisory blankets the entirety of Perlis and Kedah, alongside all three mainland districts of Penang: Seberang Perai Utara, Seberang Perai Tengah, and Seberang Perai Selatan. Perak faces widespread disruption spanning 12 districts, including Hulu Perak, Kuala Kangsar, Kinta, Kampar, Muallim, Batang Padang, Larut Matang, Selama, Kerian, Perak Tengah, Hilir Perak, and Bagan Datuk.

Across Selangor, the advisory covers Hulu Selangor, Sabak Bernam, and Kuala Selangor, alongside Petaling and Klang, two major urban districts where drainage systems were inundated during Monday’s deluge.
In the south, the alert spans Batu Pahat, Muar, Tangkak, and Kluang in Johor.

East coast states are similarly braced for stormy weather. Kelantan faces downpours across Kuala Krai, Jeli, Tanah Merah, Machang, Pasir Mas, Tumpat, Kota Bharu, Pasir Puteh, and Bachok. In Terengganu, the alert covers Besut, Hulu Terengganu, Setiu, and Dungun.

Across East Malaysia, the warning covers multiple divisions in Sarawak, including Lubok Antu in Sri Aman, Sarikei, Betong, Tanjung Manis in Mukah, Asajaya and Sebuyau in Samarahan, Marudi and Telang Usan in Miri, and Belaga in Kapit. In Sabah, the bulletin spans Ranau, Papar, Penampang, Tuaran, and Kota Kinabalu along the West Coast, alongside Tambunan, Membakut, Pensiangan, and Keningau in the Interior, Kalabakan in Tawau, and Tongod in Sandakan.

MetMalaysia issues thunderstorm advisories when satellite and radar indicators track rainfall intensity exceeding 20mm per hour that is either imminent or expected to persist beyond an hour. The department noted that these warnings serve as short-term alerts, valid for a maximum of six hours from issuance.
The alert follows Monday’s cloudburst that inundated arterial roads, submerged vehicles, and crippled the evening commute across the Klang Valley.
With ground saturation still high, authorities have urged motorists and residents in flood-prone zones to monitor real-time weather updates.
c275938385fa0dca: SINGAPORE: Actor Thomas Ong has been forced to cut short his 45-day solo holiday in Japan after fracturing his right ankle in a fall.
But the 57-year-old remains grateful that the accident will not ruin his upcoming work commitments.
Ong revealed the injury in a Facebook post on Nov 1, sharing a photo of himself in a wheelchair at the airport, with his right ankle bandaged and a pair of crutches beside him.
The accident happened on Oct 25 when he slipped on wet stone steps after taking photos of a waterfall in the light rain. At first, he thought he had only sprained it.
"I thought at that time that it was just a minor sprain. I didn't realise the injury was more serious than I'd imagined," he told Chinese-language newspaper Lianhe Zaobao.
Despite the pain, Ong drove himself to a nearby hospital, where an X-ray confirmed the ankle fracture.
Doctors offered him two options: surgery to insert a metal plate, which could get him moving again after just over two weeks, or non-surgical treatment to let the bone heal gradually.
Both options required about six weeks of recovery.
Ong said he chose to skip the surgery and the plaster cast, preferring to rest at home and let the bone heal naturally.
The recovery period overlaps with a work trip on Dec 7, when he is due to lead a tour group to Europe.

"At that moment, I didn't actually feel unlucky; instead, I felt a sense of gratitude I couldn't quite put into words," he wrote, adding that if the accident had happened two weeks later, he might have missed the trip entirely.
Although his 45-day Japanese adventure ended after just 10 days, Ong said he had no regrets as he had already enjoyed the country's scenery, hot springs, waterfalls, and local food.
Joking about his unusual souvenirs, he wrote: "The souvenirs I brought back from Japan this time are two crutches."
He ended his post with a final message: "See you next year, Japan."
48c71c2c31d0a566: PETALING JAYA: Timbalan Perdana Menteri Zahid Hamidi nafi dakwaan berniat mensabotaj kerajaan Madani berhubung pendedahan pembatalan atau penangguhan pelaksanaan projek pembangunan luar bandar di Sabah dan Sarawak.

Zahid yang juga menteri kemajuan desa dan wilayah, menjelaskan fakta berhubung penangguhan atau pembatalan pengeluaran surat setuju terima (SST) bagi projek berkenaan adalah benar, dan beliau sedia mengemukakan bukti dokumen arahan rasmi bagi menyangkal tuduhan itu.
"Saya tidak bermaksud demikian (mensabotaj), tetapi faktanya begitulah...sama ada ia ditangguh atau dibatalkan, yang jelas semua SST yang telah dan akan dikeluarkan itu diarah untuk dibatalkan.

"Saya mempunyai bukti surat arahan yang dikeluarkan. Saya boleh tunjukkan kepada Ahli Parlimen Jelutong," katanya menurut Bernama pada sidang media selepas merasmikan Majlis Jelajah Pendidikan Tinggi dan TVET Mara Peringkat Melaka di Dewan MPJ Alamanda, Jasin.

Semalam, Ahli Parlimen Jelutong RSN Rayer ketika mencelah dalam perbahasan di Dewan Rakyat mempersoalkan kenyataan dibuat Zahid berhubung pembatalan projek pembangunan luar bandar di Sabah dan Sarawak, yang disifatkan Rayer sebagai cubaan mensabotaj kerajaan Madani.

Katanya, dakwaan peruntukan projek itu dikorbankan turut mencetuskan kemarahan rakyat terhadap kerajaan Madani, sedangkan Menteri Kewangan II Amir Hamzah Azizan sudah menjelaskan tiada pemotongan dibuat.
Rayer juga mendakwa Zahid bersekongkol dengan pembangkang untuk menjatuhkan kerajaan Madani.

Minggu lalu, ketika menggulung perbahasan Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan 2027 di peringkat dasar, Zahid mendakwa beberapa projek pembangunan luar bandar bagi 2026 di Sabah dan Sarawak dibatalkan walaupun peruntukan sudah disediakan.
Katanya, arahan pembatalan itu dikeluarkan ketua setiausaha kementerian, namun beliau tidak memperincikan kementerian terbabit atau jumlah projek terjejas.
d156f8c708876293: POLITICAL understanding can be a bridge between former rivals, but it cannot become a substitute for electoral transparency.

The reported Tafahum Siasi between Barisan Nasional and Pas, involving Perikatan Nasional partners, offers Melaka an important test: can cooperation grounded in perpaduan ummah produce accountable government while respecting Malaysia's plural society?
The chronology matters. On Oct 21, BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi announced an understanding allocating 21 constituencies to BN and seven to Pas and its allies.

Following an Umno supreme council meeting on Oct 28, secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki confirmed political cooperation with Pas and PN partners, joint campaigning and plans for a common manifesto.
These announcements establish political intent, not an independently inspected contractual agreement.
More importantly, the Election Commission's Oct 31 nomination figures recorded BN candidates in 23 constituencies, PN candidates in five and Bersatu candidates in seven.
These categories cannot simply be equated with the announced 21–7 division. They expose an important distinction between negotiated allocations, registered party labels and actual nominations.
Public explanations should reconcile the numbers without pretending that an earlier political formula necessarily describes the final ballot.
Zahid's wider Musyawarah Nasional language invokes consultation and shared responsibility. Its appeal is understandable.
Political fragmentation can weaken policy continuity, divert resources into perpetual rivalry and encourage promises that outlive electoral campaigns.
Yet musyawarah is meaningful only when participants know who speaks for whom, which decisions require consent and how disagreements are resolved.
Consultation is not a ceremonial blessing bestowed after decisions have already been made.

The phrase perpaduan ummah carries religious and social significance, but its political application demands care. Muslim solidarity need not diminish the citizenship, dignity or representation of non-Muslims.
Melaka's communities deserve assurance that cooperation will strengthen inclusive administration rather than turn religious identity into an electoral dividing line.
A partnership claiming moral purpose must demonstrate fairness in public appointments, development priorities and access to services.

There is also a constitutional and institutional distinction. Pas may negotiate with BN, but a party leader's endorsement does not automatically establish the consent of every PN component or settle questions about coalition authority.
Nor does state-level coordination automatically rewrite BN's federal relationship with Pakatan Harapan.
Political actors should identify the parties bound, the scope of commitments and the procedures approving them.
Ambiguity might simplify campaign speeches; it complicates democratic accountability.

Experiences in Johor and Negeri Sembilan offer lessons, not templates. Different candidate configurations, local grievances, leadership structures and voter priorities make mechanical comparisons unreliable.
Their relevance lies in evaluating whether parties communicated alliances clearly, managed machinery responsibly and converted electoral arrangements into durable policy delivery.
The question is not whether Melaka can reproduce another state's political arithmetic, but whether it can avoid repeating avoidable governance failures.
Economic substance must now replace coalition symbolism. Families facing living costs need credible assistance, affordable housing and reliable transport.
Young people need employment pathways, skills development and investment that produces actual jobs.
Businesses need predictable licensing, infrastructure maintenance and consistent procurement rules. Rural communities need dependable utilities and accessible public services.
A joint manifesto should identify responsible agencies, funding assumptions, implementation deadlines and measurable outcomes rather than offer competing slogans beneath a shared banner.
Checks and balances remain essential even when parties coordinate electorally.
Legislative scrutiny, independent auditing, transparent tenders and accessible constituency services cannot be traded away for the convenience of political unity.
Opposition representatives retain legitimate oversight roles.

Coalition partners should likewise be free to question policy performance without being accused of betraying an understanding. Stability achieved by suppressing scrutiny is merely fragility wearing formal attire.

The understanding deserves neither automatic celebration nor reflexive condemnation. Its legitimacy depends on documented consent, accurate public communication, lawful nominations and benefits reaching all communities.
Leaders should publish the operative terms, reconcile seat announcements with confirmed candidacies and explain federal implications consistently and honestly.
Campaign speeches should state practical priorities and avoid implying that cooperation guarantees results.
Ultimately, Tafahum Siasi should be judged not by the warmth of handshakes but by the integrity of decisions.
Melaka needs consultation that precedes announcements, leadership that accepts scrutiny and policies whose outcomes citizens can measure.
Perpaduan ummah becomes politically constructive when it reinforces justice, intercommunal trust and responsible governance for everyone.
* The writer is a political and economic analyst

d3fe6c691de00923: SINGAPORE, Nov 3 — Singapore pledged to strengthen the implementation of the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (AATHP) as it prepares to assume the Chairmanship in 2027, said Sustainability and the Environment Minister Grace Fu.

She said the Republic will work towards establishing the Asean Coordinating Centre for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control (ACCTHPC) in Indonesia to strengthen cooperation and coordination in managing land and forest fires, as well as transboundary haze.
“This will only come into force after six Asean member states have ratified the establishment agreement of the ACCTHPC.

“Singapore will submit our instrument of ratification for the establishment agreement in the next few days, and we will strongly encourage other Asean member states to do so,” she said during a question-and-answer session in Parliament on Tuesday.
She was responding to questions from several Members of Parliament on how the government intends to address the transboundary haze issue at the regional level.
The session was live-streamed via the Digital Development and Information Ministry’s YouTube channel.

According to Fu, Singapore will also work with Asean member states to enhance the implementation of relevant initiatives under other Asean sectoral pillars that tackle the root causes of transboundary haze.
These include initiatives such as sustainable land and peatland management and guidelines on crop burning.
“Some Asean member states have indicated that they will raise the transboundary haze issue at the upcoming Asean meetings.
“Singapore will support these discussions and share how we intend to act against companies responsible for the haze,” she added. — Bernama
93a8c1c876bbc34b: KUALA LUMPUR: Malakoff Corp Bhd's subsidiary GB3 Sdn Bhd has commissioned and resumed commercial operations at its 429 megawatt (MW) open cycle gas turbine power plant in Lumut, Perak on Oct 7.
The milestone comes almost three months ahead of the scheduled commercial operation date of no later than Jan 1 under its new power purchase agreement (PPA) with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB).
The GB3 plant was last in service in December 2022. The new PPA will run until Dec 31, 2029.
The plant's follows the execution of new PPAs for GB3 and Segari Energy Ventures Sdn Bhd (SEV) in May 2026.

This is after Malakoff successfully secured extensions for three of its gas‑fired power plants under the Energy Commission's Project Category 1 competitive bidding exercise for new generation capacity in Peninsular Malaysia for the period 2025 to 2029.
Together with the SEV plant, which is scheduled to continue operations no later than July 1, 2027, the Lumut power plant will provide a combined 1,732MW of generation capacity to the national grid.
Malakoff's Prai power plant in Penang resumed operations on April 9.
Malakoff group chief executive officer Syahrunizam Samsudin said the plant's early return will help meet the country's growing need for reliable power.
"Electricity demand in Malaysia keeps growing as the economy expands and new investments, particularly data centres, come into the country.
"For the grid to keep up, it needs sufficient, dependable capacity that it can count on at all times.
"With GB3 back in operation earlier than scheduled, an additional 429MW is now available to support the country's energy security", he said.
Syahrunizam said bringing a power plant back into commercial operation after almost four years requires extensive planning and hard work.
"With Prai and GB3 now running, and SEV to follow next year, we are making good use of plants that have served the country well for many years."
He added that extending existing assets is a practical and cost‑efficient way to strengthen energy supply as the infrastructure is already in place.
2069fd66a5556dc3: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal today granted lawyer Mahajoth Singh leave to commence a judicial review challenging two orders issued by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) against him.
A three-member bench, comprising Justices Firuz Jaffril, Faizah Jamaludin and Ahmad Shahrir Salleh, allowed Mahajoth's appeal to set aside the High Court's decision dismissing his leave application.
Shahrir, who delivered the unanimous decision, remitted the case to the High Court to hear its substantive merits.
"In our view, the (Mahajoth's leave) application is arguable and not frivolous."
Shahrir said the High Court judge had erred in determining the relationship between Section 30 and Section 46 of the MACC Act as well as the scope of Section 126 of the Evidence Act 1950.
He said the appellate court was of the view that those questions are best addressed at the substantive hearing of the judicial review.

On Jan 30 this year, the Kuala Lumpur High Court dismissed Mahajoth's application for leave to initiate the judicial review challenging the two orders issued to him in connection with his client, businessman Albert Tei.
Mahajoth was appointed solicitor for Tei, who was detained by MACC on Nov 28, 2025.

Mahajoth is seeking a certiorari order to quash a directive compelling him to attend MACC headquarters in Putrajaya for an oral examination and to produce documents and items related to Tei as part of an investigation under Section 30(1)(b) of the MACC Act.
He claimed the orders under the MACC Act contravened the statutory protection of privileged communication between solicitor and client under Section 126 of the Evidence Act.

During the Court of Appeal proceedings, counsel N Surendran, representing Mahajoth, submitted that the issues raised are novel and ought to be heard at the substantive stage as they involve the legal position on solicitor-client privilege.

Senior federal counsel Shamsul Bolhassan, assisted by federal counsel Krishna Priya Venugopal, appearing for the attorney-general, argued that the subject matter is not amenable to judicial review, as the orders to examine the appellant and to produce documents under Section 30(1)(b) of the MACC Act are an exercise of a function in the course of a criminal investigation.
Mahajoth was also represented by several other lawyers, including Latheefa Koya, Rajesh Nagarajan and Sachpreetraj Singh.
The Malaysian Bar, which was allowed to intervene in the appeal, was represented by a team led by Anand Raj.
fa1e4a00b4932841: MADRID: Police have dismantled a protest tent camp in Madrid, authorities and activists said Tuesday, more than a month after it was set up in the centre of the Spanish capital to protest the country's housing crisis.
"The eviction of the Puerta del Sol camp took place without incident or episodes of violence," said sources from Madrid's city government, reporting that 334 people were removed and two arrested.
In a post on Telegram, protest organisers called it "a violent police operation" that left several people injured after being hit or as a result of tear gas.

The camp sprang up on September 26 following the police eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her lifelong Madrid home, after the real estate company that owned the apartment drastically raised the rent.
That sparked nationwide protests against runaway housing costs and a lack of tenant protections, with tens of thousands of demonstrators hitting the streets.

Protesters set up a tent camp in Madrid's emblematic Puerta del Sol square, with the encampment turning into a sprawling warren of tents and tarpaulin hosting hundreds of people in a mini-city equipped with a canteen, a clinic and a space for meetings.
Police moved to clear the camp overnight Monday-Tuesday, city authorities said.

"The operation involved 220 national police officers and 180 officers from Madrid's municipal police, with the participation of firefighters and social services," city sources said, welcoming "an operation that made it possible to carry out the evacuation without violent disruption to public order".
Early on Tuesday, much of the square was closed off by police, with cleaning operations underway, according to AFP journalists on the scene.
6b4a318b7c8db5a3: NEW YORK, Nov 3 — A child in New York died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 30 years, authorities said on Monday.
The child died in Lewis County in the north of New York, according to county and state health authorities.
“I am heartbroken to learn that a child in Lewis County has died after contracting measles,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement.
“As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through.”

Hochul, a Democrat, appeared to connect the death to Trump administration health policies, saying it was “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The United States is facing its worst measles outbreak in 35 years.
As of October 29, there were 4,834 cases reported in 47 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Hochul declared a disaster emergency in New York in October, following measles outbreaks in the state and neighboring states.
Measles was declared eradicated in the US in 2000 after years of effective vaccination campaigns.
But the illness has made a worrying comeback in recent years as vaccine scepticism rises alongside a growing mistrust of health authorities.
Measles causes fever, respiratory symptoms, painful rashes and, in severe cases, pneumonia and brain inflammation, which can lead to death.
The disease continues to claim tens of thousands of lives around the world every year. — AFP
43800f08157d77fe: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 —The Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) has returned investigation papers concerning allegations that Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim was forced to sign an Instrument of Proclamation to the police for further action.
In a statement today, the AGC said it had reviewed the investigation papers submitted by the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) on Oct 30 concerning the incident.

“An investigation was opened under Section 506 of the Penal Code after the Menteri Besar alleged that he had signed a proclamation concerning changes to the position of the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan under undue influence.
“Following a comprehensive review, it was found that several further steps must be undertaken by the investigating officer before any decision can be made.
“Accordingly, the investigation papers will be returned to the PDRM today for further action,” the AGC said.
Yesterday, Attorney-General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar reportedly denied any delay by the AGC in reviewing investigation papers relating to a report involving Ismail. — Bernama

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) delivered the informal guidance during meetings with investment banks over the past few days, the FT reported […]
79e8ddd3ea77d34b: KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) is investigating a Facebook account operating under the name "Vikke Lee" over content allegedly insulting the Sultan of Selangor, Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah.
In a statement today, MCMC said the content was suspected of containing highly offensive material touching on race, religion and royalty (3R), targeting the Selangor ruler.
A statement was recorded at the Sri Petaling police station to assist investigations, while a mobile phone and SIM card were seized, it said.
MCMC said it viewed seriously the dissemination of suspected false information and offensive content targeting the royal institution, particularly material that could threaten social harmony.
The case is being investigated under Section 233 of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 (Act 588).
Upon conviction, offenders face a maximum fine of RM500,000, jail of up to 2 years, or both.
MCMC also reminded the public to use social media responsibly and refrain from creating or sharing content that violates the law.
ebc149543f96311b: PETALING JAYA: Pengguna mesti dapat melihat jumlah sebenar yang perlu dibayar pada setiap peringkat urus niaga, kata Menteri Perdagangan Dalam Negeri dan Kos Sara Hidup, Armizan Mohd Ali.

Dalam jawapan bertulis di Parlimen, Armizan berkata kementeriannya memandang serius amalan mengenakan caj tambahan atau caj tersembunyi yang hanya dimaklumkan kepada pengguna pada peringkat akhir sesuatu transaksi hingga menyebabkan harga yang perlu dibayar lebih tinggi berbanding harga yang dipaparkan atau diiklankan.
"Amalan ini bukan sahaja mengelirukan, malah menjejaskan hak pengguna untuk mengetahui harga sebenar dan membuat keputusan pembelian secara telus dan bermaklumat.
"Pengguna hendaklah dapat melihat harga yang perlu dibayar, dan bukan hanya mengetahui kewujudan caj-caj tertentu di peringkat akhir transaksi," katanya.
Katanya, tindakan boleh diambil melalui Seksyen 10B(1), Akta Kawalan Harga dan Antipencatutan 2011.

Peruntukan itu mewajibkan mana-mana pihak yang mempamerkan, mengiklankan, menyiarkan atau menyebut harga barangan atau caj perkhidmatan hendaklah memasukkan dalam harga yang dipaparkan itu semua cukai, duti, cukai kerajaan dan apa-apa caj ain yang hendak dikenakan dalam harga yang dipaparkan.
Armizan berkata prinsip ini turut diperkukuh melalui Garis Panduan Pelaksanaan Dasar Harga Terangkum, khususnya bagi sektor makanan dan minuman serta transaksi e-dagang dan penghantaran.

Katanya, garis panduan itu menghendaki agar harga akhir yang dipaparkan hendaklah mengambil kira komponen seperti harga asas, caj perkhidmatan dan caj penghantaran sebelum pengguna membuat pengesahan tempahan.
Beliau berkata badan korporat yang didapati bersalah boleh didenda sehingga RM100,000, manakala individu berdepan denda sehingga RM50,000, hukuman penjara sehingga dua tahun atau kedua-duanya sekali.

Armizan berkata kementerian juga boleh mengambil tindakan di bawah Akta Perlindungan Pengguna 1999 [Akta 599], yang menetapkan bahawa peniaga boleh dikenakan tindakan sekiranya memberikan gambaran mengelirukan kepada pengguna mengenai harga barangan atau perkhidmatan.
Seksyen 9 dan Seksyen 10 Akta berkenaan turut melarang perlakuan atau representasi palsu dan mengelirukan berkaitan sifat dan ciri sesuatu barang atau perkhidmatan.
"Peruntukan ini bukan sahaja meliputi transaksi di premis fizikal, tetapi turut terpakai kepada urus niaga perdagangan secara elektronik," katanya.

Di bawah Seksyen 145 Akta 599, badan korporat yang didapati bersalah boleh didenda sehingga RM100,000, manakala individu boleh didenda sehingga RM50,000, dipenjara sehingga tiga tahun atau kedua-duanya sekali.

Kementerian itu juga menguatkuasakan Perintah Kawalan Harga dan Antipencatutan (Penandaan Harga bagi Barangan dan Caj bagi Perkhidmatan) 2020, yang mewajibkan perniagaan dan penyedia perkhidmatan memaparkan senarai perkhidmatan serta caj mereka dengan jelas dan mudah dilihat.
62684404a460dbad: BARCELONA, Nov 3 — La Liga president Javier Tebas said Monday he is maintaining dialogue with Chinese authorities in an effort to defuse a row over Kylian Mbappe’s comments about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV did not air a single La Liga match this weekend, while Real Madrid’s win at Racing Santander on Sunday was also not shown on pay television in the country.

In a clip from an interview with French show The Bridge which has since been taken down, Mbappe had said he was amused by an internet meme showing his face photoshopped onto “some guy, think he’s a Chinese dictator”, an apparent reference to Mao.
Mbappe, Real Madrid and La Liga apologised for the comment after a backlash in China, where mocking former leader Mao — blamed by historians for millions of deaths — is taboo.

“For now, we wait and see how the situation develops... because given how events have unfolded, everything depends on things calming down a bit, on all the mess easing,” Tebas told reporters at the World in Progress forum in Barcelona.
“There will be ongoing dialogue — I’m speaking with the Chinese authorities, both in Madrid and in Beijing, and we’re going to wait.”
Tebas, who held a meeting with Chinese ambassador to Spain Yao Jing last week, highlighted several strong links between China and Spanish football which could help resolve the dispute.
“We’ve had a strategy for several years now with the political and sporting authorities in China,” he explained.
Tebas met Chinese State Councillor Shen Yiqin and a high-ranking delegation at Barcelona’s La Masia youth academy facilities in February, along with Barcelona president Joan Laporta.
“With the president of China Media Group (the parent organisation of CCTV) we have a good agreement,” continued Tebas.
“He’s been to La Liga, I’ve met with him (Shen Haixiong). Every time I travel to Beijing I have a meeting with him.”

China effectively cut ties with the NBA for several years from 2019 after then-Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters, but Tebas said he was “hopeful” of reverting the current situation.
“I’m going to travel, talk, and keep talking with the Chinese authorities,” he added.
“We’ll try everything possible to normalise the situation as much as we can.”
Mbappe scored on Sunday as Real Madrid beat Racing 3-0 in La Liga to move within three points of leaders Barcelona. — AFP
7176e6f9d1e7978c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 — The success in staging the Petronas Malaysian Motorcycle Grand Prix (MotoGP) 2026 has not only strengthened the country’s reputation as a host of world-class motorsports events, but also serves as a catalyst for local economic activity, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

47872983325c2e57: The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow.

But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona.

Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior.

"We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post. "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly."
To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math.

Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold.
There was no training using gradient descent; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights.

"All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post. "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

"Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights."

Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so.
Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting, which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge.

More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment.

The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say. ®
e3b9edd9dfeaf9cc: MELAKA, Nov 3 (Bernama) -- Melaka’s previous experience of seeing chief ministers replaced within a short period should serve as a lesson to all political parties to ensure the stability of the state administration is maintained after the 16th Melaka State Election, according to former Chief Minister Adly Zahari.

“The issue is stability, not who wants to lead and so on. I think there are many ways we can use after the election. Whoever leads, our commitment is to ensure political stability,” he told Bernama.

Adly said one possible approach was the implementation of a Confidence and Supply Agreement (CSA), similar to the one at the federal level, to ensure that the government has sufficient support to govern and pass the budget if it has only a slim majority.

Adly said an inclusive approach, including providing allocations to opposition state assemblymen, was among the measures he had implemented while serving as Chief Minister to ensure that all elected representatives could carry out their responsibilities to the community.

He said that when he led the state government, an allocation of RM60,000 was provided to each opposition state assemblyman to enable them to operate service centres and appoint staff to assist local residents.

Adly is facing a four-cornered contest against Perikatan Nasional candidate Muhammad Ridzuan Mohd Sarif, Parti Bersama Malaysia candidate Dr Aliza Che Amran and independent candidate Abu Bakar Sabudin.

2883a888178fd5b0: MALAYSIA has a law to protect its critical systems. It has no law to answer when another state attacks them. Today's warning from the Prime Minister shows why that gap must close.

When Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim told the Dewan Rakyat that Malaysia is "certainly among those considered potential targets" of cyber and hybrid threats, he was describing more than crime.
He was describing the possibility of cyber warfare: hostile action, likely state-linked, aimed at disrupting a nation's infrastructure and bending its will.
He gave two reasons. Our data centre and digital capacity now rivals Europe's. And our principled stand on Palestine and Gaza has made us unpopular in some capitals.
Both are sources of national pride. Both also make us a target, at a time when attacks on portals, public registries and government systems have shaken Europe, the United States and Japan.

The government moved quickly: a special National Security Council meeting on Monday, a meeting of all departments under the Chief Secretary, a Bank Negara session with every financial institution, and a closed-door National Security Council (MKN) briefing for MPs.
These are the right first steps. But a nation cannot brief its way through a war. It needs law. And on cyber warfare, Malaysia has almost none.
Resilience without a warfare framework is incomplete
The Cyber Security Act 2024 (Act 854), in force since Aug 26, 2024, was a genuine milestone.

It created a National Cyber Security Committee chaired by the Prime Minister, gave NACSA statutory teeth, and placed duties on National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities across eleven sectors: codes of practice, risk assessments, audits and incident notification.
But it is a resilience and compliance statute. It asks whether our critical operators are secure and whether they report incidents.
It does not ask the question my doctoral research keeps returning to: what may Malaysia lawfully do when the attacker is a foreign state or its proxy, and the aim is coercion rather than theft?
Resilience is not only the ability to absorb a blow. It is also the ability to deter, respond and recover within the law. Without a cyber warfare legal framework, our resilience is half-built.

Five gaps stand out: First, no legal definition of cyber warfare. Our statutes do not distinguish a cyber crime, a cyber incident and a cyber attack by a state. Without that line, every response is improvised.

Second, no threshold or escalation ladder. There is no legal test for when a cyber operation becomes a national emergency, or when it may amount to a use of force or armed attack under international law.
Third, no attribution process. No statute says who decides that a state is behind an attack, on what evidence, and with what consequences.

Fourth, no legal basis for response. The powers of NACSA, MKN, the Ministry of Defence and the Armed Forces to respond, including lawful countermeasures and active defence, are not set out in law, and;
Fifth, no protection for civilians in cyber conflict. Our framework does not commit Malaysia, in law, to the principles of distinction and proportionality when it defends itself in cyberspace.

Estonia and Singapore treat cyber as a domain of war. Estonia learned the hard way. The 2007 attacks that paralysed its banks, media and ministries turned a small digital state into a global reference point on cyber warfare.

It folded cyber into national defence: a military cyber command, a volunteer Cyber Defence Unit within its Defence League, Nato's cyber defence centre of excellence in Tallinn, and a "data embassy" abroad so the state can keep running if its own servers fall. For Estonia, cyber resilience and cyber defence are one policy.

Singapore built its framework in layers. Its 2018 Cybersecurity Act, the model for our own, protects critical infrastructure, and a 2024 amendment extended it to cloud, data centres and other digital foundations.

But Singapore did not stop at regulation. It made Digital Defence a pillar of its Total Defence doctrine, and in 2022 created the Digital and Intelligence Service as a fourth branch of its armed forces. Its civilian resilience law sits alongside a clear military role in cyberspace.
The lesson is not to copy either state. It is that both treat cyberspace as a domain where war can be waged, and legislate accordingly. Malaysia still treats it mainly as a domain of compliance.
What a cyber warfare legal framework should contain
I propose that the government begin drafting a Cyber Warfare Legal Framework, either as a dedicated National Cyber Defence Act or as a new Part of the Cyber Security Act 2024, with these elements:

Definitions and thresholds - Define cyber attack, state-sponsored cyber operation and cyber warfare, and set a clear ladder: cyber incident, national cyber emergency, and an attack amounting to use of force or armed attack under the UN Charter.

A statutory cyber emergency regime - Set out who may declare a national cyber emergency, the powers it unlocks (binding directions to operators, mandatory information sharing, emergency takedowns), and firm sunset clauses with parliamentary oversight.

Attribution and lawful response - Create a formal attribution process led by MKN, with a legal basis for proportionate responses, from diplomatic action and lawful countermeasures to the inherent right of self-defence, consistent with international law.

A legislated chain of command - Define the roles of NACSA, MKN, the Ministry of Defence and the Malaysian Armed Forces, including the point at which a cyber attack becomes a defence matter and the Armed Forces' cyber units take the lead.

Humanitarian safeguards - Commit Malaysia in law to distinction, proportionality and precaution in cyber operations, and to the protection of hospitals, water, power and other civilian infrastructure.

Whole-of-society resilience - Widen the Act's reach to data centres, cloud and supply-chain vendors, and create a national cyber preparedness plan and a volunteer cyber reserve that draws on our universities and industry.
The Prime Minister himself pointed to the EU's whole-of-society Preparedness Union Strategy.

The framework should be reviewed alongside the Computer Crimes Act 1997, the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, the Personal Data Protection Act 2010 and the Armed Forces Act 1972, so that our laws speak with one voice.
Clear law protects both security and liberty. Emergency powers improvised in a crisis protect neither.
From a national framework to an international one
A national cyber warfare framework can harden our defences and clarify our response. It cannot stop a foreign state from attacking. That is where international law falls short.

There is still no binding treaty that clearly prohibits state cyber attacks on civilian infrastructure, or defines where espionage ends and armed attack begins in cyberspace. Voluntary norms agreed at the United Nations are a start, but they bind no one.

This vacuum invites what I call cyber colonisation: the use of digital dominance to coerce, extract from and subordinate less powerful nations. Countries of the Global South, building data centres and digital economies as Malaysia is, are the most exposed.
Malaysia is well placed to lead here. Our foreign policy is independent, our voice on justice for Gaza is heard across the Global South, and our standing in Asean is strong.
We should champion an Asean position on cyber peace and push, at the UN, for a binding international treaty that protects civilian infrastructure and outlaws cyber colonisation.
A nation that speaks for justice offline should also speak for it online.
Legislate before the attack, not after
Estonia built its cyber defence after it was attacked. Singapore built its framework before the worst could happen.
Malaysia now has a choice between those two paths, and the Prime Minister's warning today tells us there is little time to choose.

The Cyber Security Act 2024 gave us the foundation of resilience. A Cyber Warfare Legal Framework would complete it: one that defines the threat, governs our response, protects civilians, and stands for peace in a domain where the strong are tempted to rule unchecked.
We must not wait for the next attack to write the law that should have answered it.

* The writer is a PhD in Law candidate at the Ahmad Ibrahim Kulliyyah of Laws, International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM), researching the advancement of Malaysia's cyber warfare legal framework in comparison with Estonia and Singapore

ec3ee16ec851f9df: LONDON: Turning to your biggest rival is rarely a sign of confidence. Yet Qatar's decision to sign long-term contracts for US supplies suggests the world's second-largest LNG exporter is increasingly concerned that instability in the Gulf could undermine its ambitious expansion plans.
QatarEnergy last week signed a 20-year agreement to buy 3 million metric tonnes per year (mtpa) of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Woodside Energy's facilities in Louisiana.
A week earlier, it signed agreements with Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi plants through 2054.
Deliveries under the contracts begin in 2030 and 2031 and will make Qatar the largest buyer of US LNG.

QatarEnergy CEO Saad al-Kaabi told Reuters last week that he expects to sign additional supply agreements with US and other producers this year, potentially locking in millions of tonnes of overseas LNG for decades to come.
Before the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28, the state-owned company had already been expanding internationally.
It had been acquiring stakes in LNG projects from North America to Africa as part of a strategy to broaden its trading portfolio and gain greater flexibility.
The latest deals, however, reflect a more fundamental shift. Rather than simply diversifying its portfolio, Qatar now appears to be buying insurance against disruptions to its own exports.
Qatar's purchases are another sign that the US has not so quietly emerged as the biggest beneficiary of the global rethink of Middle East energy risk, marking a historical reversal of roles.

"Twenty-five years ago my White House colleagues and I worried the US would become as dependent on Qatar for LNG as we were on Opec for oil," said Bob McNally, founder and president of Rapidan Energy Group and a former White House energy advisor to president George W Bush.
"Then came the shale revolution and Iran War, and now Qatar is buying from us," McNally said.
Insurance policy

As Washington and Tehran continue to spar over the future of the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf producers are racing to reduce their reliance on the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of global energy supplies flowed before the war.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE are expanding, or preparing to expand, pipeline networks that bypass Hormuz to improve their ability to export crude oil and refined fuels outside the Gulf.
Qatar faces a far more difficult challenge.
Unlike its neighbours, the small Gulf state has no viable route for exporting LNG other than Hormuz.
Its entire LNG industry is concentrated at its giant Ras Laffan facility, where gas from the North Field is processed and shipped to customers around the world.
The conflict made those risks painfully clear in March, when an Iranian missile damaged two of QatarEnergy's 14 LNG trains at Ras Laffan, removing about 17% of the country's export capability.
QatarEnergy said the outage would cost roughly US$20 billion a year in lost revenue and that repairs would take around three years.
Any effort by Qatar to develop alternative export infrastructure would require tens of billions of dollars of investment in pipelines and liquefaction capacity.
Even then, building massive new energy facilities simply creates more sites vulnerable to attack, as the war has demonstrated.
It is therefore unsurprising that Qatar’s strategy is to seek protection not by building more domestic infrastructure but through geographic diversification.
A two-horse race
The current challenges come at a particularly difficult time for Qatar, as the Gulf state embarks on its biggest growth push in decades.

The International Energy Agency estimates that roughly 300 billion cubic metres of new LNG export capacity will come online worldwide between 2025 and 2030, increasing available global supply by around 50%.
More than half of that new capacity will come from the US, while Qatar is expected to account for roughly another quarter.
The two countries are therefore set to dominate growth in global LNG trade over the coming decade, setting up an increasingly intense competition for market share.
Qatari LNG still has some distinct benefits over US supplies, most notably production costs.
Industry estimates place Qatari costs at roughly US$3-US$5 per million British thermal units, about half the cost of many US projects.
Washington, however, enjoys one critical advantage: American LNG exporters face none of the geopolitical constraints associated with dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
This was not previously a major concern, but in the wake of the Iran war, oil and gas buyers increasingly value security of supply as highly as price.
The question is no longer whether QatarEnergy’s plans to nearly double LNG production by 2030 will remain on track.
The first new trains are expected to start operations early next year.
The question is whether those facilities will actually remain operational in a radically reshaped Gulf.

Even if the US and Iran eventually agree to a sustainable peace deal in the coming months – a big “if” – the role of Hormuz in regional energy markets has likely changed forever, to Qatar's disadvantage.
The days of guaranteed access through the waterway appear to be over.
For Qatar, then, purchasing US LNG offers a way to profit from growing demand for politically secure supplies, even if those supplies come from North America.
This may be the strongest evidence yet that the Iran conflict has accelerated the decade-long shift in energy market power away from the Middle East and toward the US.
(The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso, a columnist for Reuters.)
19fd84717af48ca4: PETALING JAYA: A mother had to fight against strong currents to save her two children from a flash flood at Kampung Melayu Subang yesterday, fearing they would otherwise be swept into a river.
Fatimah Muhammad, 43, said the floodwaters rose rapidly to chest level at her home in Jalan Merbau, while the strong currents made it difficult for them to reach safety.

Fatimah, who has lived in the village for 19 years, said heavy rain began at about 3pm before conditions worsened, forcing her to flee with her children, Nur Izzati Maisarah Rose Safizul, 15, and Shafiq Syakir, 13.

“The water rose very quickly. What was most frightening was how strong the current was. If we had not fought against it, we could have been swept into the river,” she told FMT at the relief centre at Dewan Siantan Kampung Melayu Subang.
It took them more than five minutes to reach safety before Fatimah contacted her husband, who was still at work when the incident occurred.
She described the latest flooding as one of the worst she had experienced since a major episode in 2021.
Kampung Melayu Subang has been hit by floods four times this year, including during the Hari Raya Aidilfitri celebrations in March.
For Yaman Buyar, 69, yesterday's flood nearly cost him his life after the water rose to waist level inside his home. He was eventually rescued by a resident who came to his aid in a boat.

“Thankfully, a resident came to help. Otherwise, I do not know what would have happened because I am no longer strong enough to walk to safety on my own. The flood currents were very strong,” said Yaman, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years.
Meanwhile, Taufiq Iman, 35, suffered losses of more than RM10,000 after his refrigerator, sofa and washing machine were damaged by the floodwaters.

Although his family escaped harm as they were not home when the incident occurred, Taufiq hoped financial assistance would be provided promptly to help flood victims replace damaged belongings and get their lives back on track.
For Azura Mohamad, 37, the recurring floods have also dampened her enthusiasm for buying new furniture, as she fears it could be damaged again.
“I have lost the motivation to buy household items because the floods keep recurring. I hope that once the flood mitigation project is completed, our village will no longer be flooded,” she said.
In yesterday's incident, 550 houses in Kampung Melayu Subang were affected, with an estimated 1,500 residents among those impacted.
The residents' hopes go beyond receiving assistance to replace damaged belongings. They want a long-term solution so they no longer have to live in fear every time it rains heavily.

f2574cc7e456423b: For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner.

“Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.”

“Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.”
“Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add.

Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.”
That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself.

“Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.”
The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.”
They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.”

Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do.

The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. Open-weight models become an operational expense after frontier models do the heavy lifting. ®
be2b619b03b2b76e: RIYADH, Nov 3 — Saudi oil giant Aramco on Tuesday announced a 34.6 per cent surge in third-quarter net profit, as the Middle East war keeps crude prices soaring while the kingdom’s energy infrastructure comes under regular attack.
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have targeted Saudi tankers, pipelines, storage facilities and refineries regularly since hostilities resumed in July, intensifying their strikes in recent weeks.
The kingdom has also had to contend with the Houthis and Iran hampering traffic in the straits of Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz, complicating exports.

Yet Aramco — the cornerstone of Saudi Arabia’s economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies — saw its profits soar during the third quarter thanks in large part to stubbornly high oil prices.
The firm said net profit hit 135.9 billion riyals (RM147.5 billion) in the third quarter, compared with around 101 billion riyals in the same period a year earlier.
The results come as energy majors around the world have seen earnings surge because of disruptions to oil and gas supplies in the Middle East, pushing up refining margins and prices.
But Aramco’s boss warned that the conflict continued to weigh heavily on energy security.

“Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security,” president and CEO Amin H. Nasser said in a statement.
Stripping out exceptional items, adjusted net income came in at 116.9 billion riyals.
The median analyst consensus for third-quarter adjusted net income was US$30.66 billion, according to an external estimate based on 12 analysts forecasts.

“The earning results are likely to be rosier compared (with) a year ago, when oil prices were much lower, but less promising relative to last quarter,” Robert Mogielnicki, a research fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told AFP.
In the second quarter, Aramco reported a 44 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit to 122.6 billion riyals.
The Middle East war, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, has upended global energy markets, led to the widespread drawing down of strategic reserves and spurred inflation.
And while the war rages in the Gulf, Ukrainian drones have also battered Russian energy infrastructure, prompting Moscow to ban the export of certain products — notably petrol and diesel.
Last month, the Houthis said they targeted Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds in the kingdom’s east.

Saudi officials said a building was hit in the area housing Aramco’s operations centre, while two company employees who spoke to AFP on the condition of anonymity said a tower in the headquarters was struck.
Dire straits
With the Strait of Hormuz contested, US military naval escorts have enabled millions of barrels of crude to pass through the crucial waterway each day.

Last month, US Central Command said it had helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil through the strait since the summer, and facilitated the passage of more than 3,000 commercial vessels over the past six months.
The increase in Gulf exports, however, has done little to prevent market volatility.
Oil prices tumbled more than seven per cent on Monday, as signs that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Back in the kingdom, months of uncertainty have added to economic headwinds.

Despite government revenues coming in above initial forecasts, Saudi Arabia has revised up its projected budget deficit for 2026 to 245 billion riyals, or 4.9 per cent of gross domestic product, from an initial forecast of 165 billion riyals.

Government spending is expected to exceed initial projections by 9.3 per cent, while the finance ministry forecasts the Saudi economy will contract by 3.6 per cent in 2026, driven by a 21.8 per cent decline in oil-related activity.
The kingdom expects to reduce its deficit to 191 billion riyals in 2027, or 3.6 per cent of GDP, while continuing to invest in economic diversification projects.
The IMF expects Saudi Arabia to end the year with a 3.3 per cent contraction in GDP, five percentage points lower than its previous forecast in July. — AFP

be51a9c42f567a7a: A cloud architect has created an open-source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads.

VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.”
Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms.
In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective.
Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it.

“Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.”
“I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.”

He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.”
Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code.
The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes.

In his email to The Register, Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match.

“Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register. “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.”

Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools.

OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround.
Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools. ®

76af35d96ed52712: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.

Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).

The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.

It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).

But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.
So one month in, who’s on board?

Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.

There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.

The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).

As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.
But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.

In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.
But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.

Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.
But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.

In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.

Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.

One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.

But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.

People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.

If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.

Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

AISIN thinks existing chips aren’t a good fit for such roles, because they rely on external memory to store AI models and then generate a lot of traffic between a processor and the model. That traffic, the company contends, makes image recognition and other on-device uses of AI less effective. DRAM is also currently vastly expensive.

The company’s response is a system-on-chip built on a 16nm FinFET process, an Arm Cortex A53 dual-core CPU, plus an Arm MaliG31 GPU. The chip includes built-in STT-MRAM, which stores both model weights and an operating system.

AISIN and its research partners at Tohoku University say that approach means the chip can go from power-on to kernel startup in 65.7 milliseconds – 38 times faster than is possible if using external memory – and run the Tiny YOLOv3 object detection algorithm on the chip.

“To effectively utilize the limited on-chip memory capacity, a hybrid multiplication architecture combining 8-bit and 16-bit multiplication was developed” according to a machine translation of Tohoku University’s announcement [PDF]. “By combining 16x16, 16x8, and 8x8 bit multiplication, the amount of weight data for the AI model was reduced by 53 percent, from 17.7MB to 9.36MB, while maintaining 16-bit precision.”
AISIN is an established parts supplier and already sells to Toyota and other automakers but hasn’t said if or when it can get this chip into production.

Meanwhile, the likes of Nvidia and Qualcomm very much want to sell their silicon to carmakers, and position themselves as sources of tech and AI smarts that existing automotive supply chain participants can’t match. ®
