4d54f679715f954d: Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the World Justice Project's Rule of Law Index. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “Rule of Law Index 2026” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice. That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific. Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”
Best performance: “order and security” and “absence of corruption”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score). Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth).

In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests. However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations.

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report, which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector. Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights. Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.
Worst performance: “constraints in government's power” and “fundamental rights”
Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score).

Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026. The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020, which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges. Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred. Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

The report described the “constraints in government’s power” performance as moderately to alarmingly risky, with constraints from the legislature ranking 84, judiciary 64, independent auditing and review bodies 61, non-government organizations 105, and the law 90 — the law refers to the legal framework that protects procedural justice and integrity regarding the appointment of officials and the electoral process. As for the subfactor “official sanctioned for misconduct,” which has a fair 22 ranking, some Hongkongers may consider the score too generous given that only one official has taken responsibility and resigned over the preventable Taipo Fire disaster.

A similar downward trend appears in the “fundamental rights” category, which ranked 29th in 2015, slipped to 38th in 2020, plummeted to 54th in 2021, and fell to 69th in 2026. The at-risk subfactors include security of suspects and dissidents (73), freedom of opinion and expression (105), privacy protection (86), freedom of assembly and association (115), and labor rights (66).

Hong Kong saw the shutdown of Apple Daily News and Stand News in 2021 upon the enactment of the National Security Law in 2020. The domestic Article 23 security law was enacted in March 2024 to further clamp down on “soft resistance” with the newly introduced sedition crime. Privacy rights have declined, as implementation rules for national security laws have empowered police to conduct physical searches of private property and digital devices without court warrants during national security investigations. Since 2020, NGOs, independent media outlets, and activist groups have vanished en masse amid a tightening political environment and shrinking civic space for organizational activities.
The fairly ranked subfactors are freedom from discrimination (29), rights of the accused and convicted (32), and freedom of religion (31).
Poor performance on “fundamental rights” also drags down the “open government” factor's rank (29), with its subfactor “civic participation” ranking 87 in an at-risk level.
Downgraded “civil justice” and “criminal justice”
Although Hong Kong's overall performance in civil and criminal justice remains fair, both factors have fallen from their historical high ranks of 11th and 7th to the current 20th and 23rd.
The main subfactors driving the decline in civil justice are discrimination (48) and improper government influence (56).

After the passage of Legal Aid Reforms in 2021, the number of applications to fund judicial review that challenge the government’s policy and decisions received by the Legal Aid Department dropped 60 percent from around 275 in 2016 to 110 in 2025. Of those 110 requests, the department approved only 2 cases. The overall number of judicial review cases fell from a peak of 3,899 in 2019 to 1,545 in 2022. Because most cases involve non-refoulement claims for refugee status, the government, in addition to the administrative Unified Screening Mechanism (USM) launched in 2014, introduced a special scheme in March 2025 to appoint eligible private practitioners as Deputy Judges of the Court of First Instance to handle these cases exclusively. The mechanism disposed of more than 3700 claims in 2025. Both reforms, driven by the government administration's political considerations, have negatively affected the poor and the non-citizen's access to judicial justice in Hong Kong.
The major subfactor contributing to the fall of criminal justice ranking is “government or political influence on the criminal justice system” (61).

Hong Kong’s criminal justice ranking first plunged in 2017, from 8th to 16th, after the government labeled the civil unrest in Mong Kok, dubbed the Fishball Revolution, as a riot and reactivated the colonial-era Public Order Ordinance to prosecute protesters en masse. Then, in 2021 and 2022, the ranking dropped again amid a series of speech-related prosecutions against 47 pro-democracy activists for participating in the primaries of the election of the legislature for conspiracy to subvert, Apple Daily senior executives for foreign collusion, and Stand News editors for conspiracy to publish seditious content. The recent convictions and heavy sentencing of Apple Daily’s executives, including Jimmy Lai, and former leaders over collusion, Albert Ho Chun-yan, Lee Chuek-yan and Chow Hang-tung, of the now-disbanded organizer of the June 4th candlelight vigil, Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, over inciting subversion, further downgraded the city’s criminal justice performance in 2026.

According to the Index’s insights, the global rule of law has declined for 9 consecutive years. Civic participation and the freedoms of speech and assembly each fell in over 60 percent of countries, and Hong Kong is among them. The city also sees the global trend of improper government influence that undermines civil and criminal justice.

The Rule of Law Index is particularly crucial to global financial centers; as the WJP notes, when the index scores reach 0.66, countries tend to have high sovereign credit ratings. Currently, Hong Kong’s score is 0.71 and trending down, while its Asian competitor, Singapore, ranks 14th with a 0.79 score and an upward trend. Watchdogs indicate this could be a bad sign for the city as it seeks to secure its spot as the region’s top economy.
Written by Oiwan Lam

c064ec7bcbb77124: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linux Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number
a3fc9a44cc6faef8: WASHINGTON, Nov 3 — Anthropic, one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday reported a more than 1,100 per cent surge in quarterly revenue and nearly US$900 billion (RM3.67 trillion) in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later this month.
The San Francisco-based company was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela, now its president, with AI safety as its focus.
The listing comes amid growing nervousness among investors about the huge sums being poured into AI.

Revenue reached US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier, though sales growth slowed from previous quarters amid fierce competition from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and cheaper models, many of them from China.

The company, whose stock market debut is seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last, said in an amended filing that its net loss reached US$23.3 billion in the July-September period.
The loss stemmed mostly from non-cash accounting charges linked to the company’s rising valuation, the filing showed.
Anthropic also posted an operating loss of US$567 million in the third quarter as it paid more for short-term computing capacity.
The filing said the company has committed to spend about US$895 billion, mostly on computing power, with US$70 billion of that due before September 2027.

The IPO will be a major test of the market’s faith in the AI boom, with the pool of potential investors set to widen as retail traders get their first chance to buy shares directly in a standalone AI giant.
According to several media outlets, the five-year-old company plans to raise around US$100 billion in its initial public offering, at a valuation of between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion.
That would surpass the record set in June by SpaceX, which raised US$86 billion.
Last week, concerns about AI spending triggered a sharp sell-off in big tech stocks after the latest earnings showed massive investment without clear signs of a return.

Anthropic’s roughly 400-page filing devotes more than 90 pages to risks, including those facing an industry that has seen a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.
Anthropic’s focus on safety is built into its corporate structure. It is a public benefit corporation, legally required to weigh its mission of developing AI safely alongside shareholder returns.
The co-founders, meanwhile, will hold 50.1 per cent of shareholder voting power through a single special share, leaving investors who buy on the market little say over the company’s direction.
The IPO comes as more major companies involved in the AI spending bonanza turn to the markets to finance their ambitions.

Meta and Google parent Alphabet have launched their own fundraising plans on the public markets, and Oracle said Monday it was going ahead with a US$20 billion plan despite doubts about its financial exposure. — AFP

8af2df53b3f558af: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 3 — Apple exceeded analysts’ expectations for its latest results on Monday when the iPhone-maker said it notched a “revenue record” for the July-September quarter, driven by iPhone sales and services revenue, but increased costs related to AI will drag down margins.
“We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September, said in a statement before speaking on a call with analysts Monday afternoon.
Ternus hinted at an optimistic outlook for sales of its latest products, including the foldable Duo, during the holiday season.
However, CFO Kevan Parekh warned that the company Apple’s gross marin will slow a bit in the final stretch of the year, compared to its September quarter margin of 47.9 per cent.
“We expect gross margin to be between 45 per cent and 46 per cent. This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI,” Parekh said.
In June, the company overhauled Siri, its digital assistant, through a partnership with Google, whose Gemini model was used to beef up the new Siri AI.
Apple tried to assuage investors’ concerns about rising AI costs.

“We feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities,” Parekh said.
Apple launched three new phones in September — the 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max and its first folding phone called the Duo — in addition to two new desktop computers.
In October, it also unveiled a new smart display powered by Siri AI called HomeView, as well as a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen for the first time.
In July, the company also launched Apple Upgrade, a leasing program that lets US customers pay for an iPhone or other devices in monthly installments.
Chips crunch
Long criticised for falling behind in the AI race, Apple stands to benefit from the heavy spending of its peers on data centers while keeping its own investments lean.
Analysts expected the Cupertino giant to spend US$11 billion (RM44.9 billion) in the 12 months that ended in September, when its fiscal year ends.

That’s a fraction of the annual expenditures of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, which are on track to spend more than US$700 billion on capital investment this year — roughly the size of Argentina’s or Belgium’s entire economy — much of it on AI infrastructure, according to analyst estimates.
In July, Meta said it expected to spend US$145 billion this year, nearly double what it spent in 2026.
Last week, Amazon said it expects to spend US$220 billion this year, and Microsoft said it expected to spend US$170 billion by the end of the year.
Alphabet’s latest forecast for spending is between US$195 billion to US$205 billion in 2026.
The iPhone-maker is in a legal battle with one of its close AI partners, though.
In July, Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly orchestrating a campaign to steal the iPhone maker’s trade secrets as the AI lab tries to develop its own consumer hardware device.
OpenAI’s flagship product, ChatGPT, has been integrated into Apple products since 2024. — AFP
516a4f414b98a975: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 — Malaysia’s manufacturing sector is expected to continue supporting industrial production and overall economic growth in the fourth quarter of 2026 (4Q 2026), according to MBSB Investment Bank Bhd (MBSB IB).

In a note today, MBSB said the positive outlook is supported by the strong new order growth, improving export demand and sustained hiring backed by Malaysia’s stronger-than-expected gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 5.3 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026 and a 53.7 per cent year-on-year expansion in trade in September.

“Ongoing geopolitical tensions in West Asia and elevated transportation costs could continue to exert pressure on manufacturers’ margins and contribute to higher producer price inflation moving forward,” it said. — Bernama
9de50d9e2df39599: Baru-baru ini calon muda Pakatan Harapan (PH) bagi kerusi Kuala Linggi pada PRN Melaka, menarik perhatian ramai apabila mendakwa berjaya membantu menyelesaikan masalah penalti cukai lebih RM70,000 yang menghimpit sebuah persatuan nelayan sejak beberapa tahun lalu. Kenyataan itu mengundang pelbagai reaksi. Penyokong parti menyatakan inilah generasi yang kita mahu, muda dan pantas tidak seperti pemimpin tua yang lambat, malas dan banyak main politik. Di Threads sering saya lihat Gen Z bertekak dengan Gen Y (milenial). Masing-masing mahu membuktikan generasi merekalah paling bagus. Maksudnya, kami Gen X dan Boomers ni kira dinosaurlah, kena duduk di tepi diam-diam.

Tapi benar, memang perkembangan dunia hari ini sedang menyaksikan kebangkitan politik anak muda. Di Nepal, demonstrasi besar-besaran pada September 2025 yang digerakkan anak muda akibat kemarahan terhadap rasuah, nepotisme dan sekatan media sosial akhirnya membawa kepada kejatuhan kerajaan. Walaupun Shah sendiri tergolong dalam Gen Y, naiknya dia sebagai perdana menteri tidak dapat dipisahkan daripada gelombang perubahan yang digerakkan oleh Gen Z.

Di Kenya, anak muda bangkit menentang dasar percukaian dan tekanan ekonomi. Di Madagascar, anak muda bangkit melawan kerajaan. Di Maghribi menyaksikan gerakan bernama 'Gen Z 212' mendesak kerajaan melakukan pembaharuan pendidikan dan perkhidmatan kesihatan. Seperti kesan domino, walaupun tiada kaitan di antara mereka, kebangkitan anak muda ini semakin melebar ke serata dunia.

Paling baru bulan lepas dan masih berlaku, anak muda Perancis bangkit memprotes besar-besaran isu pendidikan sehingga memberikan tekanan kepada Presiden Emmanuel Macron. Gelombang rakyat kemudiannya menjadi makin besar dan merebak sehingga menarik penyertaan mahasiswa, kesatuan sekerja dan masyarakat umum memprotes isu-isu lain juga.

Ini memperlihatkan satu fenomena di mana golongan yang selama ini sering dianggap lembik dan cepat layu seperti strawberi tiba-tiba mampu mengucar-ngacirkan kestabilan politik sebuah negara. Apakah Malaysia juga sedang bergerak ke arah itu? Nampaknya calon Kuala Linggi ini cuba membayangkan bahawa proses pengambilalihan anak muda boleh bermula.

Melihat perkembangan dunia, kita tahu protes anak muda di jalan raya bukan perkara baru tetapi perlu ditegaskan bahawa menjatuhkan kerajaan dengan mentadbir kerajaan merupakan dua perkara berbeza. Semua orang boleh marah dan turun memprotes menumbangkan kerajaan. Semua orang boleh berceramah tetapi bukan semua boleh merangka dasar, merancang belanjawan dan mengurus ekonomi. Yang dulu kaki demo, kini sudah jadi menteri pun kita dapat lihat dia masih terpinga-pinga. Yang dah berhenti jadi menteri pun kita lihat banyak bercakap di podcast komplen sana-sini walhal sewaktu jadi menteri entah apa yang dia buat, tak nampak pun hasilnya.

Sebenarnya, kemunculan pemimpin muda bukan perkara baharu dalam sejarah politik negara kita. Najib Razak menjadi Ahli Parlimen ketika berusia 23 tahun, dilantik sebagai timbalan menteri pada usia 25 tahun dan menjadi menteri besar Pahang ketika berusia 29 tahun.

'Pengantin baru' Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman pun pernah menjadi menteri belia dan sukan pada usia 25 tahun. Kini, di kementerian sama menyaksikan Mohammed Taufiq Johari, menjawat jawatan menteri dalam usia tak sampai 30 tahun. Maknanya, kebolehan orang muda memimpin memang sentiasa diiktiraf. Bezanya dulu kita tidak melabelkan seseorang mengikut generasi yang bunyinya macam bunyi model telefon pintar atau kereta. Gen itulah, gen inilah!

Sebenarnya, saya sendiri rimas dengan label dan pembahagian kategori manusia kepada Baby Boomers, Gen X, Gen Y, Gen Z, Alpha dan bermacam-macam generasi lagi. Bagi saya, label tersebut bukanlah ketetapan saintifik yang mutlak. Label generasi yang pada asalnya digunakan dalam kajian sosial ini kemudian telah menjadi alat pemasaran dalam dunia perniagaan.

Dalam dunia pemasaran, pengguna perlu dikenal pasti, dikelompokkan supaya produk dapat dijual dengan lebih berkesan. Meletakkan label pada generasi adalah satu jalan mudah untuk tujuan tersebut. Masalah yang timbul ialah apabila kategori pemasaran ini mula dianggap sebagai kebenaran fakta tentang sifat manusia. Boomers beginilah, Gen X begitulah, kononnya mereka lebih lasak tapi menjadi hamba pekerjaan. Generasi sekarang pula lebih pintarlah, tetapi lembik macam strawberi. Macam saya kata tadi, kebenaran teori itu tidak mutlak dan bergantung kepada banyak faktor.

Padahal, perbezaan yang diperdebatkan selalu ini hanya sekadar pertembungan biasa antara golongan tua dengan orang muda. Orang muda dulu pun memberontak dan mempertikaikan kewibawaan orang tua yang dirasakan sudah mula tumpul. Kita waktu muda dahulu pun rebel, mahu bebas dan bercita-cita mengubah dunia. Manakala orang tua adatnya pula sentiasa meragui keupayaan anak muda. Macam kita hari ini berat untuk menyerahkan baton kerana menganggap anak muda masih belum cukup matang dan kurang pengalaman.

Di Malaysia pula, budaya politiknya memang sudah 'begitu' sejak sekian lama. Anak muda yang mahu menjadi pemimpin kebanyakannya masih perlu melalui struktur parti yang dikuasai generasi tua. Mereka perlu mendapat restu kepimpinan, mematuhi disiplin parti dan menyesuaikan diri dengan budaya politik sedia ada ini. Pendek kata, dengan acuan politik tua, Gen Z yang berada di dalamnya pun akan kelihatan poyo dan tak menarik. Itulah yang berlaku ketika Baby Boomers, Gen X dan milenial masih muda. Mahu mengubah, bercakap lantang tentang kebangkitan anak muda tetapi akhirnya tersedut ke dalam lubang yang sama.

Apakah boleh terjadi satu gelombang di mana anak muda Gen Z beramai-ramai menyertai mana-mana parti politik besar tanah air dan melakukan 'serang hendap' mengambil alih tampuk kepimpinan lama lalu melakukan reformasi politik? Sempatkah mereka naik atau belum apa-apa mereka semua akan dicantas?

Kepada calon Kuala Linggi, saya mengalu-alukan calon muda tetapi saya kira keberkesanan seseorang pemimpin bukan diukur dengan cepat atau lambatnya mendapat tandatangan perdana menteri. Itu masih belum dianggap satu perubahan. Dan kalau itulah yang dikatakan sebagai satu kerja, ia bukanlah sesuatu yang membanggakan. Budaya surat sokongan, budaya potong barisan guna kabel politik bukan perkara baru dan bukan budaya yang sihat.

Jika Gen Z bercita-cita untuk melakukan reformasi, ia harus mempercekapkan sistem pentadbiran itu sendiri tanpa banyak kerenah birokrasi dalam menyelesaikan masalah rakyat. Jika itu berjaya, kita tak perlukan hubungan istimewa wakil rakyat dengan Perdana Menteri untuk meluluskan sebarang pekerjaan. Kita mahu kecekapan sistem itu sendiri yang memainkan peranan dengan berkesan. Itu yang harus anak muda Gen Z ubah jika berjaya menjadi perangka dasar di Dewan Rakyat.

Persoalan sama ada Gen Z mampu memimpin negara tidak boleh dijawab dengan melihat kad pengenalan, kepetahan berpidato, jumlah 'follower' TikTok atau aktif menghasilkan video. Kita memerlukan pemimpin yang memahami tanggungjawab, mempunyai keberanian membuat keputusan, menghormati institusi dan sanggup dipertanggungjawabkan apabila melakukan kesilapan. Ciri-ciri tersebut tetap ada pada sesetengah pemimpin tua kita hari ini. Sekiranya ada ahli politik dari Gen Z yang tidak memenuhi kriteria tersebut, pada saya dia hanyalah mesin baharu dengan program lama.

Sesebuah negara itu hebat kerana pemimpinnya sentiasa mempunyai idea segar, bertenaga dan bersemangat melaksanakan visinya tanpa mengira berapa pun usianya. Tetapi jika pemimpin generasi muda terus membawa perangai politik lama yang poyo dan main -main, nescaya kita tidak akan ke mana-mana. Harap muka sahaja muda, idea dan wawasannya tetap lapuk. Buat apa? Kepada calon muda Kuala Linggi, jika cita-cita anda memang mahukan perubahan, 'pak cik' sokong!

12205f0e791d641a: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Sbunker. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government. Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.

Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.
The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.
This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.

Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.
Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event.

We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications.

Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments.
The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments.

The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate.

Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities.

Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions.
Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice.
The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo.
The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities.

The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them.
We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

1a7942fb3b9f842f: Diplomacy is not always measured by grand agreements, historic handshakes or comprehensive peace settlements.
Sometimes, its effectiveness is demonstrated through small but tangible improvements in human lives.
The recent decision by Myanmar’s military authorities to begin releasing ethnic Rakhine deportees following Malaysian diplomatic pressure is one such development.
According to The Irrawaddy, the releases followed Malaysia’s intervention over the detention of individuals deported from Malaysia to Myanmar.
This is hardly a diplomatic breakthrough. Yet it is not insignificant.
It demonstrates that Putrajaya’s decision to maintain engagement with Nay Pyi Taw, despite international criticism, can produce limited but measurable results.
More baby steps are needed.
First, engagement must never be confused with endorsement.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has faced criticism for engaging Myanmar’s military leadership, particularly Senior General now President Min Aung Hlaing.
Critics argue that such engagement risks legitimising a regime responsible for widespread displacement, military violence and the destruction of democratic institutions.
These concerns are valid.

However, refusing to communicate with the authorities exercising power in Nay Pyi Taw would make it harder for Malaysia to secure detainees’ release, negotiate humanitarian access or protect vulnerable returnees.
Diplomacy requires contact, even with governments whose conduct one fundamentally opposes.
The purpose is not to confer legitimacy but to influence behaviour.
Second, the releases demonstrate the potential value of sustained diplomatic pressure.
Malaysia raised concerns about the treatment of its deportees. Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan sought clarification. Myanmar subsequently began releasing those detained.
Although this sequence does not prove that Malaysian pressure alone led to the releases, it suggests that diplomatic intervention mattered.
Malaysia did not merely accept Myanmar’s treatment of the deportees. It demanded accountability.
This is how engagement should function: dialogue accompanied by expectations, verification and humanitarian safeguards.
Third, piecemeal progress must not conceal Myanmar’s larger humanitarian catastrophe.
Without a doubt, Myanmar remains deeply fractured.
The military authorities do not exercise uncontested control over the entire country.
Ethnic armed organisations and resistance forces remain powerful actors.
Rakhine State is particularly complicated because of the continuing conflict involving the Arakan Army and Myanmar’s military.
Repatriation cannot automatically be considered safe merely because some detainees have been released.
Malaysia must distinguish between voluntary returns and deportations that expose vulnerable people to persecution, detention or forced recruitment.
The principle of non-refoulement must remain central.
Fourth, Malaysia needs stronger mechanisms to monitor returnees.
Diplomatic assurances are meaningful only when independently verified.
Malaysia should work with relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organisations to establish procedures for monitoring the welfare of those returned.
Such arrangements should protect family contact, freedom from arbitrary detention and access to humanitarian assistance.
Without verification, Malaysia risks celebrating releases without knowing whether those individuals subsequently enjoy meaningful security.
Fifth, Asean must translate Malaysia’s incremental progress into collective diplomatic action.
To be sure, the Asean Five-Point Consensus has struggled to end Myanmar’s conflict.
Nevertheless, its fundamental objectives remain relevant: reducing violence, encouraging inclusive dialogue and facilitating humanitarian assistance.
Malaysia’s bilateral engagement should complement these objectives, not replace them.
The Philippines, as Asean Chair in 2026, should consider how such diplomatic openings can strengthen regional cooperation.
Asean needs more than repeated expressions of concern.
It needs Asean’s resolve to translate principles into practical humanitarian outcomes.
Sixth, engagement must extend beyond Myanmar’s military leadership.
Malaysia should maintain communication with the National Unity Government (the Myanmar government-in-exile), ethnic armed organisations, civil society and humanitarian networks.
Myanmar’s fragmentation makes broader engagement indispensable.
A settlement negotiated exclusively with military authorities cannot guarantee acceptance throughout the country.
Malaysia must broaden and deepen its diplomatic channels without abandoning humanitarian principles.
Finally, Anwar’s approach should be judged by outcomes rather than appearances.
Malaysia cannot single-handedly resolve Myanmar’s civil war.
But neither should it abandon opportunities to secure modest improvements in human security.
The release of Rakhine deportees is encouraging, although it does not establish that Myanmar has fundamentally changed.
Further progress requires humanitarian access, independent monitoring, safeguards for returnees and eventually inclusive political dialogue.
Myanmar’s crisis cannot be resolved overnight. Yet diplomatic paralysis is not a strategy.
Malaysia must remain principled without becoming immobilised by the complexity of Myanmar’s conflict.
The journey towards peace may begin with small humanitarian concessions rather than spectacular diplomatic breakthroughs.
More baby steps are needed. But genuine, verifiable and sustainable piecemeal progress is still progress.
For Myanmar’s long-suffering people, even modest improvements in human security matter.

de929831445c05d5: Walaupun seminggu sudah berlalu saya terpanggil menulis mengenai Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan dimeterai antara kerajaan, Ahli Parlimen Bersatu, bekas Ahli Parlimen parti itu yang menyokong PMX dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Sebab? Perikatan Nasional memutuskan tidak akan ikut sama yakni tidak akan menandatangani perjanjian itu yang ramai lebih gemar guna istilah Inggerisnya iaitu CSA untuk Confidence and Supply Agreement.
Keengganan PN memeterai CSA bukanlah sesuatu yang memeranjatkan walaupun pendapat umum ialah CSA peluang perkukuh kestabilan politik negara.

Dan kestabilan politik adalah antara prasyarat penting untuk memastikan dasar kerajaan dapat dilaksanakan dengan berkesan dan manfaatnya dapat dirasai rakyat, dalam sebuah negara yang sedang berdepan pelbagai cabaran ekonomi dan tuntutan pembangunan. At least that’s how Segamat MP R Yuneswaran look at it.

PN jelas tidak bersependapat lalu tidak menerima CSA. Itu hak mereka. Cuma yang menarik bagi saya ialah rakan baik PN (khususnya dalam menghadapi PRN Melaka) iaitu Pengerusi BN Zahid Hamidi menyarankan CSA diperluas kepada lebih banyak parti sama ada daripada kerajaan atau pembangkang.

Kata Zahid apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri. Kata-kata ini buat saya tersenyum lebar. Mengapa? Jawapannya di penghujung artikel ini. Lantas pada hemat saya apa yang dikata Zahid amat menarik atas dua sebab.
Sebab pertama kerana saranan Zahid dibuat semasa PN dan BN semakin mesra. Dan apabila PN tolak CSA bererti mereka tolak juga saranan Zahid.
Sebab kedua ialah apabila Zahid berkata (saya ulang ) “apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri”.

Wakil Ummo jadi perdana menteri yang dimaksudkan kita tahu ialah Ismail Sabri Yaakob. Apa yang berlaku? Tentu ramai masih ingat. Pada September 2021, Ismail memeterai apa yang dipanggil memorandum persefahaman dan kestabilan politik dengan Anwar Ibrahim yang waktu itu ketua pembangkang.
Kata Anwar, memorandum itu menjadi kenyataan kerana sikap positif Ismail yang mengambil pendekatan berunding segera dengan pembangkang sebaik dilantik perdana menteri kesembilan.

Perlu dinyatakan memorandum itu bukan CSA per se. Ini diakui Anwar sendiri waktu itu. Apa pun dalam dokumen MoU antara Pakatan Harapan dengan kerajaan pimpinan Ismail, kerajaan menjanjikan sejumlah reformasi dalam jangka waktu tertentu dan juga berjanji untuk tidak membubarkan Parlimen sebelum 31 Julai 2022.

Sebagai balasan PH pula berjanji tidak akan menggunakan undi mereka menggulingkan Ismail atau menyekat Belanjawan 2022 selagi pembaharuan dijanjikan mengikut jadual dan pembangkang dilibatkan dalam perbincangan Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan. Di samping itu PH berjanji membantu usaha kerajaan memerangi wabak Covid-19 yang melanda waktu itu.

Put simply the MoU was a good thing for the country considering the circumstance then. Namun, Zahid dan Umno menekan Ismail untuk mengadakan pilihan raya umum dengan segera kerana berpendapat Umno sedang berada pada tahap meyakinkan untuk menang. Zahid konon mahu Ismail strike while the iron is still hot.
Tindakan Zahid dan Umno boleh dilihat sebagai tidak memberi ruang kepada Ismail menjayakan MoU beliau dengan PH.

Tekanan demi tekanan dikenakan ke atas Ismail. Menyulitkan Ismail ialah beliau sekadar seorang naib presiden Umno manakala Zahid presiden parti . Akhirnya, Ismail tidak ada pilihan melainkan tunduk akur. Parlimen dibubarkan pada Oktober 2022 dan PRU15 diadakan pada November 2022.
Dan Umno/BN mencatat prestasi paling buruk dalam sejarah mereka. Umno hanya menang 27 kerusi, MCA (2) dan MIC (1). Perkiraan Zahid meleset.

Fast forward CSA yang dimeterai 29 Okt lalu. Pada upacara tandatangan kerajaan diketuai Timbalan Perdana Menteri II Fadillah Yusof. Bukan timbalan perdana menteri I. Kita tahu siapa pemegang jawatan itu.
Mungkinkah ini kerana pendirian lalu Zahid terhadap MoU 2021 dan tindakan susulannya yang boleh dilihat sebagai bertentangan dengan semangat MoU itu?
Maka, kerana itulah saya tersenyum lebar seperti disebut tadi apabila Zahid memuji CSA 2026 dan mahu ia diperluas kepada semua parti.

6b88f6d113da6cd0: Anthropic has published a regulatory filing revealing nearly $900 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, with additional estimated payments potentially pushing the total beyond $1 trillion.

The Monday filing reports that Anthropic expects to pay nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations by September 2027, with a total of roughly $447.5 billion in commitments expected to be incurred by the end of 2030. That's assuming of course its revenues continue their upward trajectory, which the prospectus warns is far from guaranteed.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all."
"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads.

Which is to say, if Anthropic's revenues don't grow faster than its compute commitments, it could end up falling into a nasty spiral. And while Anthropic has several options, including debt and equity financing, relying on these long term could dilute existing shareholders or force the company to borrow on unfavorable terms.

Every IPO filing reads a bit like this because no company can guarantee eternal success and growth. A lot of this filing's language, as damning as it might sound, is therefore just Anthropic covering its butt.

However, even though the company is still growing steadily year-over-year, the latest filing shows revenue growth is already slowing. Between Q1 and Q2 of this year, revenues grew nearly 2.5x. Yet in Q3, Anthropic's reported revenues of nearly $17 billion represented an increase of just 46 percent from Q2. In the same period, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure costs grew 77 percent and it kept signing deals that commit it to more expenditure.
Last week, we reported that Anthropic's purchase commitments exceeded $800 billion over the next decade or so.
Anthropic now says its commitments are closer to $895 billion.

Roughly $320 billion of those commitments relate to existing contractual obligations. Another $451 billion covers leases Anthropic has signed, but that have yet to commence, with the company expecting them to begin between 2026 and 2028, although some remain subject to termination rights or other conditions.

Overall, however, Anthropic's compute spend is on track to increase substantially over the next few years. And that's not even counting the blank checks Anthropic has written to secure adequate compute, which it values at $150-$175 billion, putting Anthropic's total compute tab at somewhere north of $1 trillion.

Anthropic can't walk away from some of this spending because its deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom, which now total $437 billion, are non-cancellable. Some require payment regardless of whether Anthropic lights up a single GPU.
The AI upstart estimates that of its $895 billion in contracts, only about $213 billion worth allow it to avoid payments.

The revised S1 filing also offered insights into the company's customer base, including a major reliance on cloud service providers for distribution. The likes of Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are some of the model dev's biggest compute providers, but according to the filing, cloud marketplaces accounted for roughly 44 percent of its revenue in the nine months ended September 30.

Anthropic insists that none of its customers account for more than 10 percent of revenue. Yet reliance on hyperscalers for distribution remains a risk because they are all either actively developing competing products or provide access to models from Anthropic's rivals.

Despite all the risks in its prospectus, Anthropic believes it can become a sustainable business if it can access enough compute capacity. And by doing so, the prospectus claims AI will reshape the economy "in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet."
With so much at stake, how can humanity afford not to spend like a drunken sailor? ®

7ac6714dc0760aee: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot.

Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating.

Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.”

One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said.

Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer.

The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote.

While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted.

Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher.

One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote.
The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote.

“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post.
While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®
f8edbaaa89160776: It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light.

In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science.

The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.

26fd3c5d12f13463: The next time you see a software engineer shaping silent words with their mouth, you may have to think twice before asking if they need a mental health day – they might just be wearing a pair of smart glasses that let them talk to their computer without uttering a sound.

Subvocal is a Y Combinator-backed startup aiming to produce these glasses, and already has working prototypes to show off in YouTube videos, including one with YC partner Dave Lieb trying them out and being impressed enough to offer funding. The headset isn’t what the final version will look like, the company notes, which is good: The demo headset is obviously 3D printed and far from fashionable.

Once the final product is available it should look a lot sleeker, based on mockups on the company’s website. It’s not clear when they’ll actually be released, though the preorder page says it’ll be sometime in Q1 2027 at an early bird price of $499. It’s not clear what the final full price will be.

As for how the glasses work, the founders, Georgia Tech computer science students Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, explain in a launch post on YC that the device uses low-powered radio waves projected from the glasses toward a wearer’s face. Those waves are distorted by muscle movements and the change in a person’s face shape as they speak or simply mouth words, which the duo said can be picked up and translated into written text.

“We started working on this about four months ago after building the first version at a hackathon,” the pair explained in their YC post. “Since then, we’ve gone from a table full of electronics and antennas taped to our face to a semi-portable board and sleek glasses that can decode open-ended speech at 200+ WPM and a reasonably low error rate even at a small dataset scale.”
This is just a proof of concept, and many key details are still missing, like the accuracy rate, battery life, whether it will paired with an app, or what-have-you.
“The core thing we wanted to prove first was that the signal exists and that we can decode it,” Yadav and Kumar said.

In a Hacker News post announcing the company, Yadav and Kumar explained that they started the project during the hackathon by focusing on using EMG electrodes attached to Yadav’s face. They didn’t win the hackathon, but apparently the demo was impressive enough to earn some initial funding from San Francisco VC firm Afore Capital.
Shortly after that, the pair pivoted from EMG to RF sensing, as a commercial dictation product that required sticking electrodes to one’s face was unlikely to succeed.

“Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge,” Yadav said. “First we built an extremely low-noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face.”

They eventually got to the functional prototype they have now, and pre-trained the AI models doing the speech recognition to minimize setup time. According to the company, Lieb only had to read 20 sentences to calibrate the headset to his speech patterns.

“We think silent speech can become the next interface for interacting with computers, replacing voice and the keyboard,” the company says of its goal. “Emails, prompts, messages, code, notes, commands, all at the speed of speech without bothering anyone around you.”

With just four months of work under their belts, Subvocal could be a massive hit, ushering in a new era of silent muttering productivity for workers in a variety of industries, or it could flop as it tries to scale.
Those interested in finding out can preorder a pair now for $199, with the other $300 not due until the glasses ship. ®

a750601d7fd9cb63: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos.

Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale.

"Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation."

Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps.

To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as "Legal Zero-Days: A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and "Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System" [PDF].

The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace. Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well."
Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code.

The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications.
Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world.

To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm.

For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid.
Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made.

"We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves."
Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly.

"Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases.

"This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process."
Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit.

"I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified."
Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term.

"Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®

b91db1d100bf604d: Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23. The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.”  More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions. With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond.  From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories. Deploying today’s technologies Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy.  “We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said. The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow.  There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power.  Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario. Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO2. Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said.  Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store energy. “The pace of the transition to a renewable-energy economy will strongly rely on the availability of scalable, bulk energy-storage solutions,” said Masic. Kripa K. Varanasi, a professor in the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, is working on ways to make technologies such as emissions-plume capture at power plants economically viable.  In a panel devoted to startups with links to MITEI or MITEI member companies, speakers described moving novel energy technologies from research to commercialization: Alfredo Rivela of Adaion has developed an AI tool for electrical utilities that optimizes their use of the grid; Eddie Obropta of Raptor Maps trains drones to inspect solar farms; Michele Guarnieri’s HiBot has created a robot that detects issues in power lines; and Michael Wang of Lithios is conducting field pilots that use electrochemistry to separate lithium from low-grade brines. Successful ventures, the speakers agreed, begin with a clear customer problem that can be validated by industry users and that offers a path to scaled deployment. For industry users, “innovation is not a corporate virtue,” said Steve Hellman, managing partner at Alliance Partners. “It’s an existential requirement.” Early-stage research and basic science The conference also offered a bounty of promising early research on technologies and approaches for cutting carbon emissions. A panel on MITEI’s Seed Innovation Fund Program projects introduced MIT scientists who are separating and recycling rare earth elements; designing algorithms to decide which power plants should run to meet electricity demand; and modeling the impacts on human and natural systems of development and decarbonization. A poster session revealed the next generation of energy researchers in such fields as chemistry, architecture, aeronautics and astronautics, and computer science. Graduate students are developing a wide array of technologies for carbon mitigation and new energy systems, such as a steam electrolysis process for hydrogen production; models of end-to-end decarbonization in buildings; and designs for hydrogen- and methane-fueled aircraft. The conference highlighted the importance of fundamental science in feeding the pipeline of new energy technologies. Wednesday’s keynote speaker, Danna Freedman, the F. G. Keyes Professor of Chemistry at MIT and inaugural director of Quantum@MIT, traced scientists’ evolving capacity to harness quantum computing as a tool for solving a range of problems, including those in energy. “What we want to do at Q-MIT is solve the hard problem, and the hard problem isn’t developing these ridiculously intricate and beautiful quantum tools,” said Freedman. “It is connecting the quantum tools with the applications that will change the world.” A companion panel explored one such application: quantum sensing, which leverages fundamental physics to capture a nanoscale view of materials and their properties. For instance, Lukasz Zielinski, scientific advisor to the Integrated Sensing and Measurement Program at SLB, uses a lidar camera with single-photon detectors to identify methane plumes. Moderator Paola Cappellaro, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, described her work using diamond-based sensors for detecting tiny magnetic fields from battery current, potentially helping measure battery conditions without disturbing the battery electrically. Such quantum sensors, Cappellaro said, can be “practical and impactful.”  Data centers and public trust One critical challenge facing energy researchers and industry emerged in sessions throughout the two days: the explosive growth of AI and the energy-hungry data centers that fuel this technology. As Deepjyoti Deka, a MITEI principal research scientist, put it, “the big test for AI right now is whether AI can reduce energy usage, improve efficiency, as well as bring in innovation faster than the rate at which it is going to consume electricity to get trained and deployed.”  “New ‘hyperscale’ facilities built for artificial intelligence can use more power than entire cities,” said Steve Clemmer, director of energy research in the Climate and Energy Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, sharing a recent analysis of data center proliferation. With new facilities being 10 to even 10,000 times larger than data centers built just a decade ago, he said, wholesale electricity costs will rise, and “increased reliance on fossil fuels will result in tens of billions of dollars in health damages, and trillions in climate damages.” He noted that decision-makers can mitigate these harmful impacts through clean energy development, strong ratepayer protections, and other safeguards. Larry Susskind, the Ford Professor of Urban and Environmental Planning in the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, recommended that developers go further, and demonstrate credible benefits to communities. Ultimately, developers must accept that they can’t rush community acceptance; they have to earn it by giving residents a meaningful role in shaping projects and sharing their benefits.  “You’re going to have to proceed at the speed of trust,” said Susskind.

3509accc4d52d768: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore.

The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy.

One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience.
