4e776a100c80e4cc: Sebenarnya saya malas nak tulis pasal bendera terbalik lagi sebab dah banyak kali tulis. Tetapi, apabila saya terbaca tentang bendera Malaysia yang ‘sengaja’ diterbalikkan, maka saya rasa terpanggil untuk menjelaskan beberapa perkara tentang sikap serta pandangan saya tentang Jalur Gemilang kita. Kemudian saya rasa terpanggil juga untuk mengingatkan orang muda kita supaya jangan galak sangat pasal freedom of speech and expression sampai tak kenal saudara, keluarga dan ibu bapa.

Tergempar kita membaca pasal satu kumpulan yang dikatakan orang Malaysia di Australia telah mempamerkan kepada awam bendera Malaysia yang terbalik dan ada kata tercarik-carik. Kumpulan ini dipercayai rakyat Malaysia dari Sabah dan Sarawak yang menggelarkan diri mereka Sabah dan Sarawak Keluar Malaysia (SSKM). Perbuatan ini saya anggap ‘agak berat’ dan perlu suatu komentar terhadapnya dengan cara baik dan beradab daripada bidasan dan cemuhan media sosial yang tidak terkawal.

Pertama sekali saya ingin mengucapkan terima kasih kepada menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri dari Sabah, Mustapha Sakmud. Beliau memberi teguran dan nasihat yang beradab dan bernas maka saya harap oang di Australia itu dengar baik-baik. Jangan terlajak kata nanti masa depan binasa. Sekarang mungkin gagah di Australia tetapi sepandai tupai melompat silap hari bulan kena balik negara sendiri semula. Siapa tahu nasib kita kecuali tuhan. Jadi, kalau kita dah ada rumah dan keluarga di sesuatu corner of the world, jangan cepat-cepat perlekeh, nanti kita juga yang terpaksa mencarinya di akhir hayat.

Isu bendera yang lalu bagi saya cukup jelas semuanya tidak disengajakan. Dari Editor Sin Chew kepada Kementerian Pendidikan, kesilapan Umno dan PAS Terengganu dan juga ‘Apek Tua’ di Pulau Pinang semuanya not on purpose. Ada yang tersilap dan ada yang cuai terlepas pandang sebab tidak pergi semak kerja suruhan kita sendiri. Saya telah mencadangkan supaya kita semua maaf-maafkan dan let it go tetapi jangan ulang lagi. Walaupun ada juga orang Umno yang suka mendabik dada sebagai paling patriotik mencemuh, menghina dan mengugut pihak yang tersilap pasang bendera, saya selalu menasihatkan individu tersebut supaya bertenang dan jangan cuba cari modal politik seperti ini.

Namun demikian, orang itu mendapat banyak political mileage dengan sandiwaranya. Saya tidak nampak pula beliau bising pasal bendera terbalik yang disengajakan orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia. Mungkin sebab Sabah dan Sarawak bakal sebagai king makers dalam PRU16. Kalau Onn Hafiz Ghazi gunakan istilah selective prosecution kini kita lihat ada parti yang buat selective criticism dalam isu bendera terbalik dengan sengaja.

Kembali kita kepada orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia ini, bagaimana kita nak nasihatkan mereka selain daripada apa yang dikatakan menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri itu? Biar saya guna analogi keluarga saya sebagai nasihat dan renungan untuk hidup berkeluarga. Sabah, Sarawak dan Semenanjung adalah sebuah keluarga dari aspek politik kenegaraan. Sabah dan Sarawak telah bersama Semenanjung Tanah Melayu selama 63 tahun. Umur saya sekarang 64 tahun. Saya mempunyai seorang isteri, lima orang anak, tiga orang menantu dan empat orang cucu. Ada tiga perkara penting dalam kita hidup berkeluarga.

Pertama, jangan sekali-kali guna perkataan cerai, nyah atau get out of the family. Kalau sebolehnya jangan langsung terkeluar kata-kata itu sehingga kita menghembus nafas terakhir di dunia ini. Walau apa perit sekali pun we do not say those words. Kata pepatah Melayu air yang dicincang tidak akan putus. Wise Malays. Melayu lama memang cerdik, tetapi Melayu baharu nampak terlalu gopoh-gapah. Tuhan telah menyatukan saya dan isteri. Selepas itu tuhan kurniakan kami tiga anak perempuan dan dua anak lelaki. Akhir sekali tuhan kurniakan kami semua empat orang cucu daripada perkahwinan anak-anak perempuan kami. Anak lelaki dua orang masih eligible kalau ada yang nak apply. Memang semua perkahwinan antara dua orang manusia berbeza akan ada isu, krisis dan macam-macam cabaran. Looking back semua cabaran itu 99% adalah dari diri kita sendiri dan bukan pun pasal orang lain buat. Sungguh. Blaming others for out own shortcoming is the easiest thing in the world. Jadi, kena refleksi dalaman dulu sebelum mengata salah orang ini dan orang itu. Apabila saya sakit jantung, sakit darah perut dan melalui severe panic disorder, isteri saya was by my side every time. Ada ketika yang kita tak berduit hingga kena pinjam abang sendiri atau minta anak buat loan. Itu semua lumrah hidup. We need family. Siapa lagi yang nak tolong.

Kedua, saya membina rumah di Kajang sebagai a refuge untuk semua anak saya. Saya dah siapkan konsep lima ‘studio apartmen’ yang lengkap dengan tandas, dapur, living room dan tempat tidur selesa serta aircond setiap bilik. Saya kata kalau kamu bergaduh dengan suami atau isteri you can come back and cool off di Kajang. Saya tahu berdasarkan pengalaman saya dan isteri, you cannot avoid conflicts jadi kita kena manage ia dengan menyediakan alternative refuge dan juga tempat untuk mereka mengadu. Saya dan isteri selalu mendengar keluhan anak-anak perempuan tentang suami mereka dan selalu kami mengajukan kesabaran dan pengalaman kami sendiri. Jangan cepat kita bercerai-berai atau mengadu domba sama ada dalam keluarga manusia atau keluarga negara. We can always manage whatever conflict kalau kita tidak burn the bridge dengan sesiapa.

Ketiga adalah tempat kami sediakan untuk cucu. Cucu adalah kurniaan tuhan yang amat penting bagi kehidupan kami semua. Saya sebagai ‘atuk’ dan isteri sebagai ‘nenek’ menjadikan rumah di Kajang sebagai resort bila hujung minggu dan di hari-hari cuti sekolah panjang di mana papa dan mama dua-dua bekerja di pejabat masing-masing. Saya tidak suka cucu saya ditinggalkan bertiga tanpa penyeliaan orang dewasa. Ada juga keadaan di mana bila krisis keluarga berlaku, mereka boleh menetap secara indefinitely di Kajang sehingga krisis berlalu. Seperti juga sesebuah negara, kalau kita mempunyai krisis di tempat tinggal di luar negara maka ke Malaysia jugalah kita pulang. Maka itu jangan senang-senang menolak negara atau menyisihkannya hanya kerana satu dua isu yang boleh diselesaikan dengan masa dan hikmah.

Sebagai mesej politik, kita semua ada negara dan ada keluarga dalam negara itu. Kita semua rakyat Malaysia di Semenanjung, Sabah dan Sarawak. Ia suatu gagasan penting bagi kita semua. Memang akan sentiasa ada konflik atau isu kaum, agama, politik dan sebeban lagi tetapi jika kita teguh dalam satu famili dan ada tempat untuk berlabuh maka kedua-duanya adalah important asset bagi kita. Menterbalikkan dan mencarik bendera negara dengan sengaja adalah suatu perkara yang cukup berat bagi saya. Ia sama dengan beberapa mahasiswa yang bakar gambar perdana menteri yang saban hari bekerja kuat. Itu mungkin budaya Barat atau Australia. Mungkin kumpulan tersebut hendak bakar, carik atau menterbalikkan bendera Australia pula di bawah freedom of expression di lain hari pula? Apa makna loyalty to family dan nation kalau begitu. Apa makna perbincangan dan bertolak ansur dalam hubungan antara manusia kalau jambatan dibakar terlebih dulu? Jambatan yang runtuh tidak boleh memanfaatkan sesiapa yang mungkin ada solusi baharu di masa hadapan.
Renung-renungkanlah pepatah Melayu agar tidak membakar kelambu sebab seekor nyamuk yang dimarahkan.

6d0c83d2b64fda06: So now “gomen” employees can’t use Waze, the popular navigation app. This is a truly funny-but-not-funny situation. Somebody must have invoked some scary natural security scenarios about the dangers this US-owned, Israeli-founded company poses to our nation.

Here’s why this isn’t trivial. A company I once worked in experienced a massive computer hack. Experts from overseas were brought in to investigate. Panic reigned at the top. What I remember most from the briefings by the experts was the experts saying that everyone in the industry has either been hacked, or has been hacked and didn’t know about it.
I felt rather naked knowing somebody somewhere has a lot of detailed info about me, even if the only juicy details were about at which street corners were the best char kuey teow stalls.

It turns out one of the easiest ways to hack a human target and steal information more critical than just the locations of char kuey teow stalls is to hack their co-workers, assistants, family, friends, or football buddies and not necessarily the targets themselves.

That’s not as exciting as what happens in a James Bond movie, but rather the more plodding and low-key style of a John le Carre novel. One way or another, though, with enough cunning and guile and resources, people can find out a lot of things that others would prefer left hidden.
Why they snoop

Digital surveillance has become a massive business as well as a national security tool – checking what, when, and where we went or bought or spoke, as well as where we browsed on the internet and what social media content we generated or consumed. Artificial Intelligence has made it all easier.

The purpose of all this snooping is often just to sell you stuff, but increasingly it’s also becoming a way to control people and societies and even conduct warfare - as in the case of Elon Musk personally throttling his Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine, thus harming Ukraine’s war efforts. That was one of the reasons many European nations are building digital alternatives to what Musk and the US offer, a trend that’s only gaining speed.

They're not just looking for alternatives for the latest digital stuff, either. Many nations have begun cutting off links they have relied on for decades with nations they no longer deem reliable for software, data centres and cloud services, computer chips, critical scientific research etc.

The big powers, especially the US and China, have been manipulating each other and others for years. China, which is fast catching up with the West in digital capabilities, looks safer today by comparison, but certainly they’re playing this same game too.
The Malaysian way

After banning Waze, Malaysia took the obvious next step by recommending the use of a home-grown alternative called TuJu, an app apparently running off the same backbone as Waze, but hosting all the captured data in some secure local data centres.

I haven’t downloaded TuJu, or used it in any shape or form. I know the locations of the best char kuey teow stalls by heart and can get there come rain or shine or traffic jams or anything else, up to a haze API level of 200. I'm fine, thank you.

Of course, we’re going about this the typical time-honoured Malaysia-Boleh way. First the government declares a critical national objective – industrialisation, national security, safety, pandemic response, etc.—and then, lo and behold, there appears a ready-made Malaysian solution!

We’ve seen this all before. The secrecy behind such decisions is often at a high level. Don’t forget even a toll highway concession agreement between the government and private parties is considered a sensitive national secret. Malaysia Boleh often actually means Malaysia Tak Boleh for the rest of us.

What little I know about TuJu doesn’t give me much confidence. The names associated with it seems to be the usual cast of characters of door openers to lucrative government contracts and not quite young genius alumni of the world’s top research universities or tech corporations or research institutions.
The other way

When it comes to high-tech, especially digital ones, I’m sceptical of people of my age and generation. We’re often the generation that calls AI “A-One”, as a famous episode involving a US cabinet member – handling education of all things! – hilariously reveals.

I wouldn’t even trust myself, even if I’m actually AI personified! The only good thing I can design and develop would be maps on napkins about the aforementioned char kuey teow locations which are, if I’m honest, not that great, after all.

But I’ve thought about making my own digital contributions during these critical times because it seems any old fogey can do it. I plan to release TuDia, an app that points out where you need to go; TangTu and TangNi to tell you when you’ve arrived here or there, and TuPun and TuLah to argue or commiserate with you when you’re lost.

And why not? The needs are real and urgent. All I’m asking for is complete access to all Malaysians’ personal data with a promise not to sell it to Elon Musk or Israel under a 50-year exclusive agreement that’ll be classified as a national secret forever.
Ah, silly dreams. I think all that’ll happen to me is, as Penangites like to say, that I’ll Pi Mai Pi Mai Tang Tu Jugak.
Which may work out as the name of another app that describes life in Malaysia Bolehland.

cfed78c7b30043db: President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future.

Issued on October 28, Trump’s presidential proclamation represents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla, and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. The proclamation cites an investigation under US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick as having found that US imports of such robots “poses risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.”

b394caaea4801868: Google parent Alphabet reported its Q3 financial results on Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company's stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn't earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year.

The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story's publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day.

While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google's Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That's about a billion more than analyst guesses.
8b3ed8665efbf0d7: Stenko Vlad/Shutterstock A few years ago, the singer Billie Eilish opened up on the Howard Stern Show about how she began watching porn around age 11. “I’m so angry that porn is so loved, and I’m so angry at myself for thinking that it was ok,” she said. Eilish became addicted to porn, and it led to problems. “The first few times I had sex, I was not saying no to things that were not good,” she said. She had nightmares because the content she was watching was so violent and abusive. Online porn is a multi-million dollar business, driven by algorithms designed to keep people clicking for more. These algorithms push more and more extreme content, often for free, to people who didn’t go searching for it. This can include strangulation, exploitation or incest porn, that’s often misogynistic and racist too. “If you take incest and strangulation, we can look at content studies from the 1980s, for example, when there was hardly any of that material,” Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University in the UK, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast. “Today both incest and strangulation becomes mainstream.” In the UK, the government will ban the possession and publication of incest and strangulation porn from early November. McGlynn, who worked with civil society groups to push the regulation of extreme content, says it’s a “huge step” that sends a message about the harms of “normalising sexual violence”. McGlynn, who has written a recent book about the rise of extreme porn, says large online porn platforms are pushing people towards more and more extreme content. Their business model is to keep you engaged. They want us on the platform for as long as possible, and the way to do that is to feed you more content, not necessarily what you were looking for, but also, the more extreme, the more polarising, the more shocking content … unfortunately, that seems to be what our kind of base instincts go for and what does actually engage us to keep us searching. McGlynn says an abundance of extreme and violent porn is shaping the sex lives of young people, and it can lead to an increased risk of problematic behaviour. There’s a study that followed 16,000 young people, showing that high porn use, particularly at a young age, is a big risk factor in problematic sexual behaviour of young teenage boys. And there’s studies in Australia and the US … showing that the more porn they watch, the more strangulation they see, and then the more they identify that they act out the strangulation. 10696ec422baa2f8: The Hora 1 site is at the base of this peak of rock in northern Malawi. Chelsea Smith, CC BY-NDIn the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next? We know that ancient people lived by foraging their food from wild plants and animals, but we know a lot less about their social lives. Would there be conflict as people defended territory? Or would they choose to share? Sometimes survival depends on choosing wisely between these options. Defending a territory has a cost, and it’s not always worth it. To understand how ancient people interacted with one another, we can start by looking at the food they ate. When food resources are densely clustered in predictable ways, it makes sense to establish and maintain a territory around them. When resources are sparsely distributed, they are harder to defend. One example of territoriality in modern foraging people comes from the Okiek in the mountains of Kenya. Here, families control the crucially important activity of honey-harvesting. In contrast, foraging groups that live in places where the next meal is less predictable also tend to be less territorial. For example, until recently !Kung foragers in the arid parts of the Kalahari Desert searched for animals to hunt across wide areas, and boundaries between groups were much more fluid. A smoky torch used to harvest honey. Jessica Thompson, CC BY-ND The strategies used by the Okiek and the !Kung are different solutions to the same problem: weighing the risk of going hungry against the risk of unfriendly social encounters. Applying this principle to archaeological finds can reveal clues about ancient human social organisation. The problem is how to find food remains from the ancient past. We are archaeologists who do research in Malawi, excavating fossil animal bones and stone tools from natural shelters of rock. Our aim is to understand how early humans lived from the end of the last ice age, between 19,000 and 10,000 years ago, until the start of farming and herd-keeping just a few thousand years ago. Although no glaciers were present in tropical Malawi during the last ice age, global environments were different from today. We wanted to know more about food availability then, and how this might have affected social interactions. We focused on a large shelter called Hora 1, located on a spectacular granite mountain that emerges like a tooth from the open woodlands in northern Malawi. Traces of ancient human activity are everywhere in this area: red coloured paintings on the rock walls, stone tools made of shiny quartz, hearths, human burials and, in the layers of earth carefully excavated over several visits, hundreds of thousands of bones. These are the remnants of uncountable meals for the communities who lived here. Hora Mountain rising from the landscape of northern Malawi. Chelsea Smith, CC BY-NC Of this formidable number of broken, cooked, cut, chewed and discarded animal parts we were able to identify almost 13,000 individual fragments, collectively spanning the last 21,000 years of human occupation. We have published a paper about these fragments and what they tell us about ancient cultural boundaries related to food availability. Our findings challenge the existing view that it was mostly coastal environments that promoted boundary formation in the past. Hunting close to home Large animals can provide a meal for a large group, so when hunters encounter them, they may prefer to chase them, even if that means ignoring smaller prey. But most of the bones we found belonged to small animals: tiny antelopes, hares, monkeys, and other creatures. That suggests that large prey with a lot of meat – like zebras, wildebeest and even rhinoceroses – were not very common in this valley in the past. Although the fragments were very small, we could see that they came from everywhere in the body: limbs, torsos and heads were all present. This suggests that these animals were hunted close to the site, and the whole carcass was brought back (not just the best parts of large animals). The bones indicate that foragers at Hora 1 hunted close to home throughout the thousands of years recorded in the archaeological deposits. We confirmed this by comparing the chemistry of the local geology to chemical traces in the animal teeth: we found that they matched. The fossil tooth of a wildebeest from HOR-1, an animal that has not been recorded in modern times in this part of Malawi. The lines in the tooth are where small samples were taken for chemical analysis. Ruoyang Tu, CC BY-NC But there is a twist to this story. The animal bones were extremely fragmented, on average only the size of a little finger. Then we looked at some of the smallest and most nutrient poor bones in the skeleton: the phalanges, or finger and toe bones. Most had been broken open to recover even the smallest amounts of fatty marrow from inside. Probably food was not so abundant in this valley if people spent their time on such meagre packages of nutrients. So why didn’t people just range further to find more food, and what kept them at that site for so long? We think the answer lies in their social worlds. In-group cooperation and out-group hostility We found that animals were of different ages when they died: youngsters, adults, and even animals so old their teeth were worn down. This suggests some form of indiscriminate mass hunting such as the use of nets or traps. It is also possible that fire was used to aid communal game drives of larger animals. All these practices would have required coordination of labour, as well as social norms on how to split the bounty. This in-group cooperation likely came with some sense of shared identity, like a cultural group. The next question is how far across the landscape this group would have roamed. Were they like the !Kung, who maintain strong social ties with neighbouring groups? Or were they more like the Okiek, focused on keeping resources within their families? A clue came from an unexpected source: ancient DNA. DNA preserved in some of the human burials found at these sites showed that relatedness became smaller very quickly as one moved further from the sites. Starting 19,000 years ago, at the end of the ice age, an invisible boundary was taking shape in tropical Africa, separating “us and them”. Ancient human DNA was recovered from ancient foragers buried at Hora 1 and at this cave, which is about 100km north of the Hora 1 site. Jacob Davis, CC BY-NC All this evidence together points to behaviour that was very “local” in nature. However, the focus on recovering every scrap of food suggests that prey were not abundant enough to justify active defence of this territory. We also do not see evidence for persistent violent encounters or large, stable settlements, as have been documented near rich sources of food such as lakes and oceans. It is possible that these boundaries were only symbolically defended, for instance through collective practices like the 9,500-year-old funerary pyre that we recently described from Hora 1. Read more: Oldest known cremation in Africa poses 9,500-year-old mystery about Stone Age hunter-gatherers Most “cultural groups” that are known from archaeology are inferred from durable artifacts that preserve well, such as ornaments made of animal teeth and shells, or pottery shaped in a specific way. But most foragers spent so much time on the move that they never made such heavy things. In tropical Africa, our research has unearthed evidence for ancient cultural boundaries even without these objects. We have also found that there can be a “home” territory and a strong sense of in-group cultural belonging without violence against other groups. Finally, we have shown that the vast interior of the continent, while less studied than its coasts, is a rich source of information on the evolution of human cooperation and competition. Alex Bertacchi received funding for this research from the US National Science Foundation. Jessica C. Thompson has received funding for excavations at the Hora 1 site from the National Geographic Society, Wenner-Gren Foundation, Emory University, and Yale University.
e6f6442f7057ac5e: When people view sexualised images of women, they tend to remember them less well than sexualised images of men; a quirk of memory that psychologists link to objectification. But in our new study, my colleagues and I found an unlikely “fix” – applying a mild electrical current to the forehead. Objectification means seeing someone as a body, or a set of body parts, rather than as a whole person. Our results, published in Social Neuroscience, suggest this bias in perception is not hard-wired and can be changed – at least for a while. Psychologists measure it with an upside-down test. People are much better at recognising faces and bodies the right way up – typically about 80% right, against 55% upside down – because we take in how all the parts fit together. With objects, such as houses, turning them over matters far less, because we recognise them by their parts. A 2012 study used this test on sexualised images. Volunteers briefly saw a photo, then had to pick it out from a pair: the photo itself and its mirror image. Men and women alike did far better with men in underwear when the photos were upright, but did about as well with women in similar poses either way – the pattern expected for objects. The finding has been debated, and some attempts to repeat it have failed. But a 2022 analysis pooling results from 41 papers found the “upright advantage” – how much better people recognise someone the right way up than upside down – is smaller for sexualised women than sexualised men. Sexually objectified women are seen as less competent and less fully human, and women who absorb this view of themselves tend to have poorer body image and worse mental, physical and sexual health. Exposure to sexualised media is also linked to greater tolerance of sexual violence against women. The bias also shifts with circumstances. In a 2015 study, blurring out women’s chests and groins, or describing them as medical graduates raising money for cancer research, made people recognise their bodies more like men’s. Power plays a part. In earlier research in Canada, a colleague and I asked people to spend ten minutes writing about a time they had power over someone, or when someone had power over them. An established way to make people feel powerful or powerless. Women who felt powerful showed the object-like pattern for sexualised men, and powerful men showed it for sexualised women. People who felt powerless showed the upright advantage for both. Power, rather than gender itself, may be central to objectification. Where the brain stimulation idea came from The idea of trying brain stimulation came from my lab’s work on a famous illusion. In the Thatcher illusion, first shown with a photo of the former British prime minister, a face with its eyes and mouth turned upside down looks grotesque the right way up but almost normal upside down. Turning “Thatcherised” faces upside down also hurts recognition much less than it does with ordinary faces – just as with sexualised women. We had found that the same weak current made Thatcherised faces easier to recognise the right way up, bringing back the usual difference. Would it do the same for sexualised women? The Thatcher illusion. In our new study, 76 university students tried to memorise photos of male and female models posing in underwear – half of them upside down. They then saw the same photos again, each the same way up as before and mixed with 32 new ones, and said whether they had seen each one before. Half the students received a weak current for ten minutes, using a technique called transcranial direct current stimulation. The others received a placebo that switched off after 30 seconds – a standard way of mimicking the tingle of the real thing. Neither the students nor the researchers testing them knew who got which. The placebo group showed the familiar pattern. They remembered men far better when the photos were upright than when upside down. For women, the difference was much smaller, mainly because they remembered upright women less well than upright men. In the stimulated group, recognition of upright images of women improved, and the gap between images of men and women disappeared. The current did not change the upright advantage for images of men. Why? Our best explanation comes from a theory of how people learn to see. With experience, the brain learns to play down features that all faces share and to pick out the details that tell one person from another. But some shared features grab attention instead, such as the flipped eyes and mouth of a Thatcherised face – or, we suspect, the body parts on display in sexualised images. They crowd out the details that tell one person from another. The current may weaken that pull. Our study was a single lab session with university students, and we only measured its immediate effects, not attitudes or behaviour. Because every image was sexualised, we also cannot say how much of the gap comes from sexualisation itself rather than other differences between the photos. Brain stimulation is no cure for sexism. But if ten minutes of a weak current – or ten minutes spent writing about feeling powerful or powerless – can shift how people see a body, objectification looks less like a fixed feature of human vision and more like a habit. And habits, unlike hard-wiring, can change. Ciro Civile receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council and previously from the European Union Horizon
e5d6004b39bc62dd: Some local papers that were on the verge of extinction, like the Solon Economist in Iowa, have teamed up with universities as a way to get staffing and support. Photo from Teri Finneman, CC BYCatherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024. But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa. It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets. These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston. We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis. Knowing your community These experiments come against a grim backdrop. Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years. But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists. How the University of Iowa stepped in to save the Solon Economist. Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work. Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently. In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers. The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff. “They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.” Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines. Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships. Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.” “People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.” Chris Umscheid, editor of the Solon Economist, says the paper’s mission remains serving the community by reporting local news, but now with more staff. Teri Finneman, CC BY The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger. Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000. Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.” A $10 deal Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo. Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up. How the Oglethorpe Echo found a new owner. “I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.” NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership. In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added. The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed. Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county. The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds. She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit. When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester. Amanda Bright’s journalism students at The University of Georgia rotate across different roles to develop writing, editing and multimedia skills. Teri Finneman, CC BY The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said. But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat. But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said. Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added. Service over profits One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships. The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances. These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting. Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view. “Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.” Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U." Pamela E. Walck does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
76b1fc93db730851: A frequent complaint about the U.S. healthcare system is that predicting how much your care will cost is notoriously difficult. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision via Getty ImagesImagine you get hit by a car. An ambulance brings you to the nearest hospital. Your private health insurance covers emergency care, but the hospital isn’t in your plan’s network. Before 2022, if you received emergency care from an out-of-network provider or hospital, you could get hit with an extra, often huge bill on top of what you owe as a copay, coinsurance or deductible. A law called the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, was designed to protect people with private health insurance from just these situations. It limits your costs to what you would have paid if the ambulance had brought you to an in-network hospital or you were treated by an in-network provider instead. As a health policy researcher and a former federal employee who helped draft the rules to implement the No Surprises Act, I applaud the law’s success in preventing patients from being hit with surprise medical bills in most cases. However, a small number of out-of-network providers are using the law to extract enormous payments from health plans. This behavior is starting to drive up the cost of coverage for both employers and individuals. In my view, if left unaddressed, these increases will only get steeper. Medical bill concerns The No Surprises Act was designed to address a troublesome feature of the U.S. healthcare system: It is notoriously difficult to predict how much your healthcare will cost. This is especially true when someone receives out-of-network care. Before the law went into effect, roughly 20% of inpatient emergency department visits resulted in a surprise bill from an out-of-network provider. Surprise bills are common for other types of care too. One study found roughly 40% of air ambulance rides resulted in a surprise bill, costing an average of almost US$20,000. The threat of these bills exacted an enormous emotional and financial toll. Roughly two-thirds of Americans reported being very or somewhat worried about unexpected medical bills, according to a 2020 poll conducted by KFF, a national health policy nonprofit. In some situations, you really can’t check whether your doctor is in-network. Security from surprises The No Surprises Act protects Americans from certain instances of a practice called balance billing, in which an out-of-network hospital or doctor asks you to pay the difference between what they billed for a service and what your insurance agreed to pay for it. When a provider joins your plan’s network, they agree to accept a specific payment for a given service or procedure. They agree to charge you only for cost sharing, such as a copayment, coinsurance or deductible, and they aren’t allowed to balance bill you. However, plans can’t prevent out-of-network providers or facilities from balance billing. On top of that, your own plan may also charge you a higher copayment, coinsurance or deductible when you go out of network. That’s why out-of-network care can be much more expensive than in-network care. The No Surprises Act protects consumers from these extra costs in cases where they have little or no control over whether they see an in- or out-of-network doctor. The law prohibits balance billing and requires cost sharing to be at approximately in-network levels in three cases where surprise medical bills were common: If you receive out-of-network emergency care at a hospital or independent freestanding emergency facility. In a medical emergency, you’re not expected to figure out whether the closest hospital is in-network. You can’t be balance billed. If an out-of-network provider treats you during a visit to an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center. For example, if an out-of-network anesthesiologist cares for you during a surgery at an in-network hospital, that anesthesiologist cannot balance bill you. If you receive out-of-network air ambulance services. The No Surprises Act doesn’t prevent big, unexpected medical bills in all cases. For example, you can still get balance billed for ground ambulance services or if you see an out-of-network doctor outside of a hospital or ambulatory surgical center. Providers win big The No Surprises Act is working as promised for patients – as of September 2026, it has prevented approximately 50 million surprise medical bills. But there’s a downside: Employers and unions are raising the alarm that the No Surprises Act is increasing the cost of providing health insurance. What’s driving up costs is an arbitration process run amok. Rather than specifying how much insurance plans should pay out-of-network providers, the law allows providers who are dissatisfied with the plan’s payment to bring disputes to arbitration. Each side submits an offer. The arbitrator must select one party’s offer as the out-of-network payment. To choose an offer, the arbitrator considers information submitted by both parties. Information can vary by case. But the law requires the arbitrator to always consider an amount that is basically the middle amount the health plan pays in-network providers for the same service. Health policy experts like me anticipated most disputes would be settled close to this amount. Over time, experts expected this would put downward pressure on the cost of healthcare and result in payments to both in- and out-of-network providers going down. The Congressional Budget Office predicted these lower payments would reduce premiums for consumers by 1% and reduce federal deficits by $17 billion. If insurers are charged big bucks by out-of-network providers, they will likely pass on the cost to consumers in the form of higher premiums. krisanapong detraphiphat/Moment via Getty Images As a federal employee, I worked on rules that would have required the arbitrators to treat the middle amount as a strong benchmark. I expected those rules to achieve savings like those predicted by the Congressional Budget Office. But lawsuits from providers blocked those rules from going into effect. Without those rules, arbitrators are selecting offers that are far above what plans would pay in-network. The winning offers are also much larger than what Medicare would pay for the same service. Providers are winning the vast majority – roughly 85% – of these disputes. They are also using arbitration more than expected. The federal government estimated there would be 17,000 disputes annually. Last year, there were more than 2 million disputes, many brought by providers with private equity investment. And the volume of disputes has grown every year. Frequent and big provider wins at arbitration will not put downward pressure on healthcare prices. They will likely do the opposite. Consumers bear the cost When a provider wins an arbitration dispute, an individual patient’s cost sharing doesn’t change. It is capped at what the in-network amount would have been. However, consumers as a group are the ones who ultimately will pay for the cost of arbitration. Researchers estimate the arbitration process alone cost health plans $22.4 billion in the law’s first four years. This doesn’t include the increases in in-network rates that are likely to occur if arbitration trends continue on pace. I’m concerned that to pay for this, insurance companies will increase rates. Employers will need to budget more to pay for health insurance or increase the amount their employees pay. We’re already seeing the costs of arbitration affect the price of health insurance. The New York state employee plan reported that the No Surprises Act was a key driver behind the plan’s 10% rate hike for 2027. A Texas city reported the No Surprises Act caused its employee plan to exceed its 2026 budget by $40 million. Right now, only a small portion of providers use arbitration. If volume continues to grow and providers continue to win big, the cost of arbitration will grow as well – and so too will costs for consumers. Looking forward With healthcare costs a huge concern for Americans and a major issue in the 2026 midterm elections, the No Surprises Act is under scrutiny. Congress appears interested in addressing this threat to affordability. In September 2026, the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee hosted a roundtable to discuss options to fix the law. In October, U.S. Rep. Frank Pallone, a New Jersey Democrat, introduced legislation to scuttle the arbitration system entirely. Absent action by Congress, I fear that the protection the No Surprises Act offers Americans will come at a cost that ultimately limits consumers’ access to health insurance. Lindsey Murtagh receives funding from Arnold Ventures

Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability.
​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.
Here’s what needs to change.
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot

Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.
—James Temple
This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries

Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.

The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.
Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise.

0c49eb4fc30298f0: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.

The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.

Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.

OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.

Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.

AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.

Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.

No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.

Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

73686718715a7fd8: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.
